nodes.name: Triangle removal lemma
nodes.statement: For any epsilon > 0, there exists delta > 0 such that any n-vertex graph G with fewer than delta n^3 triangles can be made triangle-free by removing at most epsilon n^2 edges.
assumptions: For any epsilon > 0
conclusions: there exists delta > 0 such that any n-vertex graph G with fewer than delta n^3 triangles can be made triangle-free by removing at most epsilon n^2 edges.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{thm:dense-triangle-removal} 
For any $\epsilon > 0$, there exists $\delta > 0$ such that any $n$-vertex graph $G$ with fewer than $\delta n^3$ triangles can be made triangle-free by removing at most $\epsilon n^2$ edges.

nodes.name: Weak regularity lemma for dense graphs \cite{frieze1999quick, lovasz2007szemeredi}
nodes.statement: Let (X, P_X), (Y, P_Y) be finite probability spaces (with full sigma-algebras), f : X times Y to C, and varepsilon in (0, 1). Then there exist partitions P of X and Q of Y, each with at most 2^O(1/varepsilon^O(1)) parts, such that \[ leftvert leftvert f - E(f mid P otimes Q) rightvertrightvert_substack \\ square le varepsilon ||f||_L^infty. \] (Here we denoted P otimes Q := \A times B : A in P, B in Q\, and the conditional expectation E(f mid P otimes Q) is obtained by averaging f over parts of P otimes Q; see crefsubsec:partitions.)
assumptions: Let (X, P_X), (Y, P_Y) be finite probability spaces (with full sigma-algebras), f : X times Y to C, and varepsilon in (0, 1).
conclusions: Then there exist partitions P of X and Q of Y, each with at most 2^O(1/varepsilon^O(1)) parts, such that \[ leftvert leftvert f - E(f mid P otimes Q) rightvertrightvert_substack \\ square le varepsilon ||f||_L^infty.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{thm:weak-dense-regularity} 
Let $(X, \mathbf{P}_X), (Y, \mathbf{P}_Y)$ be finite probability spaces (with full $\sigma$-algebras), $f : X \times Y \to \mathbf{C}$, and $\varepsilon \in (0, 1)$. Then there exist partitions $\mathcal{P}$ of $X$ and $\mathcal{Q}$ of $Y$, each with at most $2^{O(1/\varepsilon^{O(1)})}$ parts, such that
\[
    \left\vert \left\vert f - \mathbf{E}(f \mid \mathcal{P} \otimes \mathcal{Q})
    \right\vert\right\vert_{\substack{ \\ \square}} \le \varepsilon ||f||_{L^\infty}.
\]

(Here we denoted $\mathcal{P} \otimes \mathcal{Q} := \{A \times B : A \in \mathcal{P}, B \in \mathcal{Q}\}$, and the conditional expectation $\mathbf{E}(f \mid \mathcal{P} \otimes \mathcal{Q})$ is obtained by averaging $f$ over parts of $\mathcal{P} \otimes \mathcal{Q}$; see \cref{subsec:partitions}.)

nodes.statement: The crucial feature of crefthm:regularity-intro is the strength of the uniformity norm, which can get arbitrarily close to that of the density norm. This is possible because the Schatten q-norms essentially interpolate between a measure of density (when q le 2) and a measure of uniformity (when q = infty). Naturally, the bound for the entropies H(P), H(Q) blows up as r approaches q.

nodes.statement: Unless specified otherwise, all graphs mentioned in this paper are finite, unweighted, undirected, and simple. We denote by V(G) and E(G) the sets of vertices and edges of a graph G; thus the elements of E(G) are two-element subsets of V(G). We define mathbbm1_G : V(G) times V(G) to \0, 1\ by setting mathbbm1_G(x, y) = 1 iff \x, y\ in E(G), and we write e_G(V, W) := sum_x in V, y in W mathbbm1_G(x, y) for any V, W subset V(G). Here are some particular graphs: item For k ge 3, we denote by C_k the cycle of length k (with k vertices and k edges). item For k ge 1, we denote by P_k the path of length k (with k+1 vertices and k edges). item For s, t ge 1, we denote by K_s,t the complete bipartite graph on s + t vertices (e.g., K_2,2 cong C_4). We also distinguish between several meanings for counting instances of a graph in another graph: item[(1).] By the number of copies of a graph H in a graph G (or simply the number of H's in G), we mean the number of subgraphs of G which are isomorphic to H. item[(2).] We write textnormalInj(H, G) for the number of injective copies of H in G, i.e.\ the number of monomorphisms from H to G (or embeddings of H in G). item[(3).] We write textnormalHom(H, G) for the number of homomorphic copies of H in G, i.e.\ the number of homomorphisms from H to G. Formally, we write \[ textnormalHom(H, G) := sum_x_v in V(G), forall v in V(H)\ prod_\u, v\ in E(H) mathbbm1_G(x_u, x_v), \] \[ textnormalInj(H, G) := sum_x_v in V(G), forall v in V(H)\ mathbbm1_x_u neq x_v,forall u neq v prod_\u, v\ in E(H) mathbbm1_G(x_u, x_v). \] Hence when V(G) is equipped with the uniform probability distribution, crefeq:Schatten-2k implies that forall k in Z_ge 2 : textnormalHom(C_2k, G) = n^2k ||mathbbm1_G||_S^2k^2k.

\label{not:graphs}
Unless specified otherwise, all graphs mentioned in this paper are finite, unweighted, undirected, and simple. We denote by $V(G)$ and $E(G)$ the sets of vertices and edges of a graph $G$; thus the elements of $E(G)$ are two-element subsets of $V(G)$. We define $\mathbbm{1}_G : V(G) \times V(G) \to \{0, 1\}$ by setting $\mathbbm{1}_G(x, y) = 1$ iff $\{x, y\} \in E(G)$, and we write $e_G(V, W) := \sum_{x \in V, y \in W} \mathbbm{1}_G(x, y)$ for any $V, W \subset V(G)$. Here are some particular graphs:
\begin{itemize}
    \item For $k \ge 3$, we denote by $C_k$ the cycle of length $k$ (with $k$ vertices and $k$ edges).
    \item For $k \ge 1$, we denote by $P_k$ the path of length $k$ (with $k+1$ vertices and $k$ edges).
    \item For $s, t \ge 1$, we denote by $K_{s,t}$ the complete bipartite graph on $s + t$ vertices (e.g., $K_{2,2} \cong C_4$).
\end{itemize}
We also distinguish between several meanings for counting instances of a graph in another graph:
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(1).] By the number of \emph{copies} of a graph $H$ in a graph $G$ (or simply the number of $H$'s in $G$), we mean the number of subgraphs of $G$ which are isomorphic to $H$. 
    \item[(2).] We write $\textnormal{Inj}(H, G)$ for the number of \emph{injective copies} of $H$ in $G$, i.e.\ the number of monomorphisms from $H$ to $G$ (or embeddings of $H$ in $G$).
    \item[(3).] We write $\textnormal{Hom}(H, G)$ for the number of \emph{homomorphic copies} of $H$ in $G$, i.e.\ the number of homomorphisms from $H$ to $G$.
\end{itemize}
Formally, we write
\[
    \textnormal{Hom}(H, G) := \sum_{x_v \in V(G), \forall v \in V(H)}\  \prod_{\{u, v\} \in E(H)} \mathbbm{1}_G(x_u, x_v),
\]
\[
    \textnormal{Inj}(H, G) := \sum_{x_v \in V(G), \forall v \in V(H)}\  \mathbbm{1}_{x_u \neq x_v,\forall u \neq v} \prod_{\{u, v\} \in E(H)} \mathbbm{1}_G(x_u, x_v).
\]
Hence when $V(G)$ is equipped with the uniform probability distribution, \cref{eq:Schatten-2k} implies that
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:2k-cycles}
        \forall k \in \mathbf{Z}_{\ge 2} : \qquad 
        \textnormal{Hom}(C_{2k}, G) = n^{2k} ||\mathbbm{1}_{G}||_{S^{2k}}^{2k}.
    \end{equation}

\label{thm:sparse-removal-odd-cycles}
For any $\epsilon, K, C > 0$ and integer $k \ge 2$, there exist $n_0, \delta, \tau > 0$ such that the following holds. Let $n \ge n_0$, $p > 0$, and $G$ be an $n$-vertex graph such that
\[
    \textnormal{Hom}(C_{2k}, G) \le C p^{2k} n^{2k} \qquad \text{and} 
    \qquad 
    \textnormal{Inj}(C_{2k+1}, G) \le \delta p^{2k+1} n^{2k+1}.
\]
Suppose that for any partition of $V(G)$ into parts $V_1, V_2, \ldots$ with at least $\tau n$ elements each, a total of at most $\epsilon p n^2/8$ edges of $G$ lie between `dense' pairs $(V_i, V_j)$ with $i \neq j$ and $e_G(V_i, V_j) \ge K p |V_i| |V_j|$. Then $G$ can be made $\{C_3, C_5, \ldots, C_{2k+1}\}$-free by removing at most $\epsilon pn^2$ edges.

nodes.name: Extremal numbers and quasi-smooth families
nodes.statement: Given positive integers m, n and a family of bipartite graphs F, we denote by textnormalex(n, F) (respectively, textnormalex(m, n, F)) the maximal number of edges in a graph on n vertices (respectively, a bipartite graph on m+n vertices) which is F-free, meaning that it contains no (injective) copies of any graph in F. We then say that F is (alpha, beta)-quasi-smooth for some reals 2 > alpha > beta ge 1 iff for n ge m ge 1, one has \[ textnormalex(m, n, F) ll m n^alpha - 1 + n^beta. \]
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:quasi-smooth}
Given positive integers $m, n$ and a family of bipartite graphs $\mathcal{F}$, we denote by $\textnormal{ex}(n, \mathcal{F})$ (respectively, $\textnormal{ex}(m, n, \mathcal{F})$) the maximal number of edges in a graph on $n$ vertices (respectively, a bipartite graph on $m+n$ vertices) which is $\mathcal{F}$-free, meaning that it contains no (injective) copies of any graph in $\mathcal{F}$. We then say that $\mathcal{F}$ is $(\alpha, \beta)$-quasi-smooth for some reals $2 > \alpha > \beta \ge 1$ iff for $n \ge m \ge 1$, one has
\[
    \textnormal{ex}(m, n, \mathcal{F}) \ll m n^{\alpha - 1} + n^\beta.
\]

nodes.statement: For any graph H, q in [1, 2), C > 0 and epsilon in (0, 1), there exists \[ delta ge exp left(- O_H,q,Cleft(epsilon^-O_H,q(1) right) right) \] such that the following holds. If textnormalHom(H, G) le delta n^|V(H)|, then one remove at most epsilon n^2 edges from G to eliminate all homomorphic copies of H.

\label{thm:super-dense-removal}
For any graph $H$, $q \in [1, 2)$, $C > 0$ and $\epsilon \in (0, 1)$, there exists 
\[
    \delta \ge \exp \left(- O_{H,q,C}\left(\epsilon^{-O_{H,q}(1)} \right) \right)
\]
such that the following holds. Let $G$ be an $n$-vertex graph satisfying $||\lambda^G||_q \le C n$, where $(\lambda^G_i)_{i \ge 1}$ are the eigenvalues of $G$'s adjacency matrix. 
If $\textnormal{Hom}(H, G) \le \delta n^{|V(H)|}$, then one remove at most $\epsilon n^2$ edges from $G$ to eliminate all homomorphic copies of $H$.

nodes.name: Averaging matrices
nodes.statement: Let (X, P_X) be a finite probability space, and let (x_i)_1 le i le |X| be an ordering of the elements of X. Then for any partition P of X, we define the matrix A_P in [0, infty)^n times n (which also implicitly depends on P_X and on the chosen ordering (x_i)_i) by \[ (A_P)_i,j := fracsqrtP_X(x_i)P_X(x_j)P_X(P), & exists\ P in P :\ x_i, x_j in P, \\ 0, &otherwise. \] Hence A_P is a block-diagonal matrix with |P| diagonal blocks, the sum of the squared entries in each block being 1, and each block having rank 1 (in particular, textnormalrank (A_P) = |P|).
nodes.raw_latex:
Let $(X, \mathbf{P}_X)$ be a finite probability space, and let $(x_i)_{1 \le i \le |X|}$ be an ordering of the elements of $X$. Then for any partition $\mathcal{P}$ of $X$, we define the matrix $A_{\mathcal{P}} \in [0, \infty)^{n \times n}$ (which also implicitly depends on $\mathbf{P}_X$ and on the chosen ordering $(x_i)_i$) by
\[
    (A_{\mathcal{P}})_{i,j} := \begin{cases}
    \frac{\sqrt{\mathbf{P}_X(x_i)\mathbf{P}_X(x_j)}}{\mathbf{P}_X(P)}, & \exists\ P \in \mathcal{P} :\ x_i, x_j \in P, \\
    0, &\text{otherwise}.
    \end{cases}
\]
Hence $A_{\mathcal{P}}$ is a block-diagonal matrix with $|\mathcal{P}|$ diagonal blocks, the sum of the squared entries in each block being $1$, and each block having rank $1$ (in particular, $\textnormal{rank} (A_{\mathcal{P}}) = |\mathcal{P}|$).

\label{lem:averaging-matrices}
Fix finite probability spaces $(X, \mathbf{P}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathbf{P}_Y)$, as well as orderings of their elements. With the understanding that $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{R}$ are partitions of $X$ and $\mathcal{Q}$ is a partition of $Y$, the following hold true.
\begin{itemize}
    \item[$(i)$.] For any $f : X \times Y \to \mathbf{C}$, one has
    \[
        \textnormal{Mat}(\mathbf{E}(f \mid \mathcal{P} \otimes \mathcal{Q})) = A_{\mathcal{P}} \textnormal{Mat}(f) A_{\mathcal{Q}}.
    \]
    \item[$(ii)$.] If $\mathcal{R}$ is finer than or equal to $\mathcal{P}$, then
    \[
        A_{\mathcal{P}} A_{\mathcal{R}} = A_{\mathcal{R}} A_{\mathcal{P}} = A_{\mathcal{P}}.
    \]
    In particular, one has $A_{\mathcal{P}}^2 = A_{\mathcal{P}}$, so $A_{\mathcal{P}}$ is a projection. Another consequence of this is that $(A_{\mathcal{R}} - A_{\mathcal{P}})^2 = A_{\mathcal{R}} - A_{\mathcal{P}}$, so $A_{\mathcal{R}} - A_{\mathcal{P}}$ is also a projection.
    \item[$(iii)$.] For any complex matrix $M$ with $|X|$ rows, denoting $||A||_{S^2} := \textnormal{Tr}(A A^*)^{1/2}$ for now, one has
    \begin{equation} \label{eq:energy-increment-matrices}
        ||(A_{\mathcal{R}} - A_{\mathcal{P}})M||_{S^2}^2 = ||A_{\mathcal{R}} M||_{S^2}^2 - ||A_{\mathcal{P}} M||_{S^2}^2.
    \end{equation}
    \item[$(iv)$.] The nonzero singular values (and eigenvalues) of $A_{\mathcal{P}}$ consist of $|\mathcal{P}|$ ones. If $\mathcal{R}$ is finer than $\mathcal{P}$, then the nonzero singular values (and eigenvalues) of $A_{\mathcal{R}} - A_{\mathcal{P}}$ consist of $|\mathcal{R}| - |\mathcal{P}|$ ones.
\end{itemize}

nodes.statement: Given q in [1, infty) and a matrix M in C^m times n with singular values sigma_1 ge sigma_2 ge ldots ge sigma_min(m,n), we define its Schatten norms by \[ ||M||_S^q := left(sum_j=1^min(m,n) sigma_j^qright)^1/q qquadand ||M||_S^infty := max_1 le j le min(m,n) sigma_j. \]

Given $q \in [1, \infty)$ and a matrix $M \in \mathbf{C}^{m \times n}$ with singular values $\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \ldots \ge \sigma_{\min(m,n)}$, we define its \emph{Schatten norms} by
\[
    ||M||_{S^q} := \left(\sum_{j=1}^{\min(m,n)} \sigma_j^q\right)^{1/q}
    \qquad\text{and}\qquad 
    ||M||_{S^\infty} := \max_{1 \le j \le \min(m,n)} \sigma_j.
\]

nodes.statement: Given q in [1, infty], finite probability spaces (X, P_X), (Y, P_Y), and a function f : X times Y to C, we define the q-Schatten norm of f by \[ ||f||_S^q := ||textnormalMat(f)||_S^q, \] Note that this does not depend on the chosen ordering of the elements of X and Y (implicit in the notation textnormalMat(f)), since permutation matrices are unitary.

\label{lem:Schatten-norms-functions}
Given finite probability spaces $(X, \mathbf{P}_X)$, $(Y, \mathbf{P}_Y)$, a function $f : X \times Y \to \mathbf{C}$, and $q, q_i \in [1, \infty]$, the following hold true.
\begin{itemize}
    \item[$(i)$.] $|| \cdot ||_{S^q}$ defines a norm on functions from $X \times Y$ to $\mathbf{C}$, which satisfies the same monotonicity and interpolation properties as in \cref{lem:Schatten-norms-matrices}. Moreover, $||f^T||_{S^q} = ||f||_{S^q}$.
    \item[$(ii)$.] When $q \in 2\mathbf{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$, one can rewrite $||f||_{S^q}$ as in \cref{eq:Schatten-2k} and \cref{eq:Schatten-infty}. In particular, one has $||f||_{S^2} = ||f||_{L^2}$, $||f||_{S^4} = ||f||_{\substack{ \\ \square^2}}$, and $||f||_{S^\infty} \ge ||f||_{\substack{ \\ \square}}$.
    \item[$(iii)$.] For any $A \subset X$ and $B \subset Y$, and any partitions $\mathcal{P}$ of $X$ and $\mathcal{Q}$ of $Y$, one has
    \[
        \max \left(||f \mathbbm{1}_{A \times B}||_{S^q} ,\ ||\mathbf{E}(f \mid \mathcal{P} \otimes \mathcal{Q})||_{S^q}\right) \le ||f||_{S^q}.
    \]
    Moreover, $\textnormal{Mat}(\mathbf{E}(f \mid \mathcal{P} \otimes \mathcal{Q}))$ has at most $\max(|\mathcal{P}|, |\mathcal{Q}|)$ nonzero singular values; in particular, the constant function $\mathbbm{1}_{X \times Y}$ has $||\mathbbm{1}_{X \times Y}||_{S^q} = 1$.
    \item[$(iv)$.] \emph{(Cycle counting inequality)}
    Let $k \in \mathbf{Z}_{\ge 2}$ and suppose that $\sum_{i=1}^k \frac{1}{q_i} \ge 1$.
    For $i \in \mathbf{Z}/k\mathbf{Z}$, let $(X_i, \mathbf{P}_i)$ be finite probability spaces and $f_i : X_i \times X_{i+1} \to \mathbf{C}$. Then one has
    \[
        \left\vert \mathbf{E}_{x_1, \ldots, x_k} \prod_{i=1}^k f_i(x_i, x_{i+1}) \right\vert 
        \le 
        \prod_{i=1}^k ||f_i||_{S^{q_i}}.
    \]
\end{itemize}

\[
    ||\widetilde{f}||_{S^q} = \frac{1}{|G|} ||\widehat{f}||_{q}.
\]

It thus suffices to show that the singular values of M are precisely the absolute values of the Fourier coefficients of f. Indeed, the inverse Fourier transform identity implies that for any chi in widehatG, one has \[ f(x+y) = frac1|G| sum_chi chi(x) widehatf(chi) chi(y), \] which translates to the identity of |G| times |G| matrices (noting that |G| = |widehatG|) \[ M = U D U^T, where: U_x,chi = chi(x), D_chi_1, chi_2 = widehatf(chi_1) mathbbm1_chi_1 = chi_2. \] Moreover, the matrices U and U^T are unitary by standard properties of the Fourier transform. Hence M M^* = U D D^* U^*, which is a diagonalization of MM^*, and thus the singular values of M are the square roots of the diagonal entries of D D^*, i.e., |widehatf(chi)| for chi in widehatG.

Since the maps $x \mapsto ax$ and $y \mapsto by$ are automorphisms of $G$, and permutations of the rows and columns of a matrix preserve its singular values, we have
\[
    ||\widetilde{f}||_{S^q}

where $M$ is the matrix with entries $M_{x,y} = f(x+y)$ (for some ordering of the elements of $G$). It thus suffices to show that the singular values of $M$ are precisely the absolute values of the Fourier coefficients of $f$. Indeed, the inverse Fourier transform identity implies that for any $\chi \in \widehat{G}$, one has
\[
    f(x+y) = \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{\chi} \chi(x) \widehat{f}(\chi) \chi(y),
\]
which translates to the identity of $|G| \times |G|$ matrices (noting that $|G| = |\widehat{G}|$)
\[
    M = U D U^T,
    \qquad\quad \text{where:}\qquad\quad  
    U_{x,\chi} = \chi(x),
    \qquad 
    D_{\chi_1, \chi_2} = \widehat{f}(\chi_1) \mathbbm{1}_{\chi_1 = \chi_2}.
\]
Moreover, the matrices $U$ and $U^T$ are unitary by standard properties of the Fourier transform. Hence $M M^* = U D D^* U^*$, which is a diagonalization of $MM^*$, and thus the singular values of $M$ are the square roots of the diagonal entries of $D D^*$, i.e., $|\widehat{f}(\chi)|$ for $\chi \in \widehat{G}$.

nodes.name: Generalized $L^2$ energy
nodes.statement: Fix a finite probability space (X, P_X) and an ordering of its elements. For any complex matrix F with |X| rows, any integer ell ge 1, and any partition P of X, we define the (left) ellth L^2 energy of P with respect to F by \[ E_F,ell(P) := ||A_P F_ell||_S^2^2, \] where F_ell can be defined inductively by F_1 := F and F_ell+1 := F_ell F_ell^*. In other words, \[ F_ell := F, & ell = 1, \\ (FF^*)^2^ell-2, & ell ge 2. \] We also define the total ellth L^2 energy of F by E_M,ell := ||F_ell||_S^2^2. Given another probability space (Y, P_Y) and a function f : X times Y to C, we define E_f,ell(P) := E_textnormalMat(f),ell(P) and E_f,ell := E_textnormalMat(f),ell.

\label{def:generalized-L2-energy}
Fix a finite probability space $(X, \mathbf{P}_X)$ and an ordering of its elements. For any complex matrix $F$ with $|X|$ rows, any integer $\ell \ge 1$, and any partition $\mathcal{P}$ of $X$, we define the (left) $\ell$th $L^2$ energy of $\mathcal{P}$ with respect to $F$ by
\[
    \mathcal{E}_{F,\ell}(\mathcal{P}) := ||A_{\mathcal{P}} F_\ell||_{S^2}^2,
\]
where $F_\ell$ can be defined inductively by $F_1 := F$ and $F_{\ell+1} := F_\ell F_\ell^*$. In other words,
\[
    F_\ell := 
    \begin{cases} 
        F, & \ell = 1, \\
        (FF^*)^{2^{\ell-2}}, & \ell \ge 2.
    \end{cases}
\]
We also define the \emph{total} $\ell$th $L^2$ energy of $F$ by $\mathcal{E}_{M,\ell} := ||F_\ell||_{S^2}^2$. Given another probability space $(Y, \mathbf{P}_Y)$ and a function $f : X \times Y \to \mathbf{C}$, we define $\mathcal{E}_{f,\ell}(\mathcal{P}) := \mathcal{E}_{\textnormal{Mat}(f),\ell}(\mathcal{P})$ and $\mathcal{E}_{f,\ell} := \mathcal{E}_{\textnormal{Mat}(f),\ell}$.

\[
\begin{aligned}
    ||A_{\mathcal{R}_X} F A_{\mathcal{R}_Y} - A_{\mathcal{P}_X} F A_{\mathcal{P}_Y}||_{S^{2^\ell}}
    &\le 
    ||(A_{\mathcal{R}_X} - A_{\mathcal{P}_X})F A_{\mathcal{R}_Y}||_{S^{2^\ell}}
    +
    ||A_{\mathcal{P}_X} F (A_{\mathcal{R}_Y} - A_{\mathcal{P}_Y})||_{S^{2^\ell}}
    \\
    &\le 
    ||(A_{\mathcal{R}_X} - A_{\mathcal{P}_X})F||_{S^{2^\ell}}
    +
    ||F (A_{\mathcal{R}_Y} - A_{\mathcal{P}_Y})||_{S^{2^\ell}}
    \\
    &=
    ||(A_{\mathcal{R}_X} - A_{\mathcal{P}_X})F||_{S^{2^\ell}}
    +
    ||(A_{\mathcal{R}_Y} - A_{\mathcal{P}_Y})F^T||_{S^{2^\ell}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
By symmetry, it now suffices to show that
\[
    ||(A_{\mathcal{R}_X} - A_{\mathcal{P}_X})F||_{S^{2^\ell}} \le \left(\mathcal{E}_{F,\ell}(\mathcal{R}_X) - \mathcal{E}_{F,\ell}(\mathcal{P}_X) \right)^{1/2^\ell}.
\]
But by \cref{eq:halfing} and \cref{eq:ignore-averaging}, for $1 \le j \le \ell-1$ we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
    ||(A_{\mathcal{R}_X} - A_{\mathcal{P}_X}) F_j||_{S^{2^{\ell+1-j}}} &= ||(A_{\mathcal{R}_X} - A_{\mathcal{P}_Y}) F_j F_j^* (A_{\mathcal{R}_X} - A_{\mathcal{P}_X})||^{1/2}_{S^{2^{\ell-j}}}
    \\
    &\le ||(A_{\mathcal{R}_X} - A_{\mathcal{P}_X}) F_{j+1}||^{1/2}_{S^{2^{\ell-j}}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
By inducting on $j$, this implies that
\[
    ||(A_{\mathcal{R}_X} - A_{\mathcal{P}_X}) F||_{S^{2^\ell}} \le ||(A_{\mathcal{R}_X} - A_{\mathcal{P}_X}) F_{\ell}||^{1/2^{\ell-1}}_{S^{2}},
\]
and we can further write, by \cref{eq:energy-increment-matrices},
\[
\begin{aligned}
    ||(A_{\mathcal{R}_X} - A_{\mathcal{P}_X}) F_{\ell}||_{S^2}^2
    =
    ||A_{\mathcal{R}_X} F_{\ell}||_{S^2}^2 - 
    ||A_{\mathcal{P}_X} F_{\ell}||_{S^2}^2
    = \mathcal{E}_{F,\ell}(\mathcal{R}) - \mathcal{E}_{F,\ell}(\mathcal{P}).
\end{aligned}
\]
Putting the last two equations together, we obtain our conclusion.

If $\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{D}) = \mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T})$ (i.e., the energy function is constant), then we can easily pick $\mathcal{P} = \mathcal{T}$, for example. Otherwise, let $\mathcal{P} \in \mathscr{P}$ be a partition which maximizes the real quantity
\[
    \mathcal{E}(\mathcal{P}) - \varepsilon\ \mathcal{C}(\mathcal{P}) \left(\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{D}) - \mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T})\right).
\]
Then by comparing the optimizer $\mathcal{P}$ to the trivial partition $\mathcal{T}$, we find that
\[
    \mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T}) \le \mathcal{E}(\mathcal{P}) - \varepsilon\ \mathcal{C}(\mathcal{P}) \left(\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{D}) - \mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T})\right)
    \le 
    \mathcal{E}(\mathcal{D}) - \varepsilon\ \mathcal{C}(\mathcal{P}) \left(\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{D}) - \mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T})\right),
\]
and thus $\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{P}) \le 1/\varepsilon$. Moreover, given any $\mathcal{Q} \in \mathscr{P}$, by comparing $\mathcal{P}$ to $\mathcal{P} \vee \mathcal{Q}$ we find that
\[
    \mathcal{E}(\mathcal{P}) - \varepsilon\ \mathcal{C}(\mathcal{P}) \left(\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{D}) - \mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T})\right)
    \ge 
    \mathcal{E}(\mathcal{P} \vee \mathcal{Q}) - \varepsilon\ \mathcal{C}(\mathcal{P} \vee \mathcal{Q}) \left(\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{D}) - \mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T})\right),
\]
which, combined with the subadditivity of $\mathcal{C}$, yields $\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{P} \vee \mathcal{Q}) - \mathcal{E}(\mathcal{P}) \le \varepsilon\ \mathcal{C}(\mathcal{Q}) \left(\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{D}) - \mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T})\right)$.

nodes.statement: Intuitively, creflem:energy-optimization finds a partition P with a good balance of energy and complexity: it captures most of the energy needed for applications (in the sense that small refinements of P only see a small increase in energy), while having bounded complexity. Here are some concrete objects that can fulfill the abstract roles of C, E and P from creflem:energy-optimization: item One can take C(P) to be log |P|, or the entropy H(P) (by crefeq:entropy-inequalities); Tao uses both in . item If Omega is a probability space and f : Omega to C is an L^2 random variable, one can take E(P) to be the L^2 energy E[E(f mid P_1 otimes P_2)^2]. In this case, one can regard the optimizer E(f mid P_1 otimes P_2) as the best approximation to f (of a certain type) with not too many different values. item Alternatively, given a partition P_0 of Omega (e.g., induced by a discrete random variable f), one can take E(P) to be the mutual information I(P_0 : P) = H(P_0) + H(P) - H(P_0 vee P); this is essentially what Tao does in . In this case, one can regard the optimizer P as the best approximation to P_0 (of a certain type) with bounded complexity. item For a logarithmic and relative version of the energy E(P), see crefsec:sharp-regularity. item If Omega = X times Y, one can let P consist of all partitions of the form P otimes Q, where P is a partition of X and Q is a partition of Y. This is often the case in the proof of regularity lemmas (see crefsec:sharp-regularity), but we will actually end up using Omega = X and Omega = Y separately.
nodes.raw_latex:
Intuitively, \cref{lem:energy-optimization} finds a partition $\mathcal{P}$ with a good balance of energy and complexity: it captures most of the energy needed for applications (in the sense that small refinements of $\mathcal{P}$ only see a small increase in energy), while having bounded complexity. Here are some concrete objects that can fulfill the abstract roles of $\mathcal{C}$, $\mathcal{E}$ and $\mathscr{P}$ from \cref{lem:energy-optimization}:
\begin{itemize}
    \item One can take $\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{P})$ to be $\log |\mathcal{P}|$, or the \emph{entropy} $\mathbf{H}(\mathcal{P})$ (by \cref{eq:entropy-inequalities}); Tao uses both in \cite{tao2005szemer}.
    \item If $\Omega$ is a probability space and $f : \Omega \to \mathbf{C}$ is an $L^2$ random variable, one can take $\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{P})$ to be the $L^2$ energy $\mathbf{E}[\mathbf{E}(f \mid \mathcal{P}_1 \otimes \mathcal{P}_2)^2]$. In this case, one can regard the optimizer $\mathbf{E}(f \mid \mathcal{P}_1 \otimes \mathcal{P}_2)$ as the best approximation to $f$ (of a certain type) with not too many different values.
    \item Alternatively, given a partition $\mathcal{P}_0$ of $\Omega$ (e.g., induced by a discrete random variable $f$), one can take $\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{P})$ to be the \emph{mutual information} $\mathbf{I}(\mathcal{P}_0 : \mathcal{P}) = \mathbf{H}(\mathcal{P}_0) + \mathbf{H}(\mathcal{P}) - \mathbf{H}(\mathcal{P}_0 \vee \mathcal{P})$; this is essentially what Tao does in \cite{tao2005szemer}. In this case, one can regard the optimizer $\mathcal{P}$ as the best approximation to $\mathcal{P}_0$ (of a certain type) with bounded complexity.
    \item For a logarithmic and \emph{relative} version of the energy $\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{P})$, see \cref{sec:sharp-regularity}.
    \item If $\Omega = X \times Y$, one can let $\mathscr{P}$ consist of all partitions of the form $\mathcal{P} \otimes \mathcal{Q}$, where $\mathcal{P}$ is a partition of $X$ and $\mathcal{Q}$ is a partition of $Y$. This is often the case in the proof of regularity lemmas (see \cref{sec:sharp-regularity}), but we will actually end up using $\Omega = X$ and $\Omega = Y$ separately. 
\end{itemize}

\label{lem:modify-spectral}
Given finite probability spaces $(X, \mathbf{P}_X)$, $(Y, \mathbf{P}_Y)$, and $f : X \times Y \to \mathbf{C}$, one has
\[
    ||f||_{S^\infty} \le \sup_{g,h}^* \left\vert \mathbf{E}_{x,y}[f(x,y)g(x)h(y)]\right\vert,
\]
where the supremum is over all functions $g : X \to \mathbf{C}$, $h : Y \to \mathbf{C}$ with $L^2$ norms at most equal to $3$, and values from $\{0\} \cup \{2^k, i2^k, -2^k, -i2^k : k \in \mathbf{Z}_{\ge 0}\}$. In particular, viewing such $g$ and $h$ as random variables, one has
\[
    \mathbf{H}(g) + \mathbf{H}(h) \ll 1.
\]

nodes.statement: Let \(X_i, P_i)\_1 le i le m be finite probability spaces, 1 le q_t < r_t le infty, i_t, j_t in \1, ldots, m\ and f_t : X_i_t times X_j_t to C for t in \1, ldots, k\, and varepsilon in (0, 1). Then there exist partitions P_i, P_i' of X_i such that max_i log |P_i| ll_k,q frac1varepsilon^alpha(q,infty), max_t leftvert leftvert f_t - E(f_t mid P_i_t otimes P_j_t) rightvertrightvert_substack \\ square le varepsilon max_t ||f_t||_S^q_t, respectively max_i H(P'_i) ll_k,q,r frac1varepsilon^alpha(q,r), max_t leftvert leftvert f_t - E(f_t mid P'_i_t otimes P'_j_t) rightvertrightvert_S^r_t le varepsilon max_t ||f_t||_S^q_t, where q := max_t q_t, r := q min_t (r_t/q_t), and alpha(q,r) := 2^max(lceil log_2 q rceil, 1)/(1 - fracqr).
assumptions: Let \(X_i, P_i)\_1 le i le m be finite probability spaces, 1 le q_t < r_t le infty, i_t, j_t in \1, ldots, m\ and f_t : X_i_t times X_j_t to C for t in \1, ldots, k\, and varepsilon in (0, 1).
conclusions: Then there exist partitions P_i, P_i' of X_i such that max_i log |P_i| ll_k,q frac1varepsilon^alpha(q,infty), max_t leftvert leftvert f_t - E(f_t mid P_i_t otimes P_j_t) rightvertrightvert_substack \\ square le varepsilon max_t ||f_t||_S^q_t, respectively max_i H(P'_i) ll_k,q,r frac1varepsilon^alpha(q,r), max_t leftvert leftvert f_t - E(f_t mid P'_i_t otimes P'_j_t) rightvertrightvert_S^r_t le varepsilon max_t ||f_t||_S^q_t, where q := max_t q_t, r := q min_t (r_t/q_t), and alpha(q,r) := 2^max(lceil log_2 q rceil, 1)/(1 - fracqr).

nodes.statement: Ultimately, we will only use crefthm:regularity for functions f with values in [0, infty), but it is not much harder to treat all complex-valued functions. Also, our sparse regularity method will only use crefeq:spec-norm-bound, but the cut norm bound in crefeq:cut-norm-bound may be of independent interest to the reader (e.g., since it fits better with the counting lemmas of ). While Schatten norms are stronger than cut norms, the drawback of using crefeq:spec-norm-bound is that it only controls the entropies H(P'_i) (which could be much smaller than log |P'_i|). However, this disadvantage can be removed if one is allowed to disregard a small number of elements of each X_i, which is the case for most applications.

Ultimately, we will only use \cref{thm:regularity} for functions $f$ with values in $[0, \infty)$, but it is not much harder to treat all complex-valued functions. Also, our sparse regularity method will only use \cref{eq:spec-norm-bound}, but the cut norm bound in \cref{eq:cut-norm-bound} may be of independent interest to the reader (e.g., since it fits better with the counting lemmas of \cite{conlon2021regularity,conlon2021graphs}). 

While Schatten norms are stronger than cut norms, the drawback of using \cref{eq:spec-norm-bound} is that it only controls the entropies $\mathbf{H}(\mathcal{P}'_i)$ (which could be much smaller than $\log |\mathcal{P}'_i|$). However, this disadvantage can be removed if one is allowed to disregard a small number of elements of each $X_i$, which is the case for most applications.

However, this disadvantage can be removed if one is allowed to disregard a small number of elements of each X_i, which is the case for most applications.

nodes.name: Proof of \cref{thm:regularity}
nodes.statement: We first note that it suffices to consider the case when all r_t = infty, since Schatten norms can be interpolated. Indeed, assuming that crefeq:spec-norm-bound holds when all r_t = infty, one can apply it for 2^1/(1-fracrq)varepsilon^1/(1-fracqr) in place of varepsilon (for any given r in (q, infty)); this yields partitions P'_i with \[ max_i H(P'_i) ll_q frac12^alpha(q,infty)/(1-fracrq)varepsilon^alpha(q,infty)/(1 - fracqr) ll_q,r frac1varepsilon^alpha(q,r), \] such that \[ max_t ||f_t - E(f_t mid P'_i_t otimes P'_j_t)||_S^infty le 2^1/(1-fracrq) varepsilon^1/(1-fracqr) max_t ||f_t||_S^q_t. \] But then, given any values r_t in (q_t, infty] and setting r := q min_t(r_t/q_t), creflem:Schatten-norms-functions implies that if M := max_t ||f_t||_S^q_t, then for each t in \1, ldots, k\ one has \[ &||f_t - E(f_t mid P'_i_t otimes P'_j_t)||_S^r_t \\ &le ||f_t - E(f_t mid P'_i_t otimes P'_j_t)||_S^q_t^q_t/r_t cdot ||f_t - E(f_t mid P'_i_t otimes P'_j_t)||_S^infty^1 - q_t/r_t \\ &le left(||f_t||_S^q_t + ||E(f_t mid P'_i_t otimes P'_j_t)||_S^q_tright)^q_t/r_t cdot left(2^1/(1-fracrq)varepsilon^1/(1-fracqr) Mright)^1 - q_t/r_t \\ &le left(2Mright)^q_t/r_t cdot 2^-q_t/r_tvarepsilon M^1 - q_t/r_t \\ &= varepsilon M. \] After this reduction, it remains to find partitions P_i which satisfy crefeq:cut-norm-bound, and P_i' which satisfy crefeq:spec-norm-bound for r = r_t = infty. For now, fix some partitions P_i and P_i' of X_i, which will be chosen later via the abstract energy optimization argument in creflem:energy-optimization; it will take some work to explain how exactly this optimization argument will be applied. By crefeq:cut and creflem:modify-spectral, we can express the uniformity norms of interest (for t in \1, ldots, k\) as ||f_t - E(f_t mid P_i_t otimes P_j_t)||_substack \\ square = sup_substackg_1 : X_i_t to \0,1\ \\ g_2 : X_j_t to \0,1\ |E_x_1,x_2[(f_t - E(f_t mid P_i_t otimes P_j_t))(x_1,x_2)g_1(x_1)g_2(x_2)]|, \\ ||f_t - E(f_t mid P'_i_t otimes P'_j_t)||_S^infty le sup_substackh_1 : X_i_t to C \\ h_2 : X_j_t to C^* leftvert E_x_1,x_2[(f_t - E(f_t mid P'_i_t otimes P'_j_t))(x_1,x_2)h_1(x_1)h_2(x_2)]rightvert, where x_1 is sampled from (X_i_t, P_i_t), x_2 is sampled from (X_j_t, P_j_t), and sup_h_1,h_2^* has the same meaning as in creflem:modify-spectral. In particular, all functions involved in both suprema have ||g_u||_L^2 ll 1 and ||h_u||_L^2 ll 1, while each g_u in the first supremum takes at most two values, and each h_u in the second supremum has H(h_u) ll 1 (for u in \1, 2\). Taking a maximum over t and suppressing dependencies on x_1, x_2 for notational simplicity, we get max_t in \1, ldots, k\ ||f_t - E(f_t mid P_i_t otimes P_j_t)||_substack \\ square = sup_substackg^t_1 : X_i_t to \0,1\ \\ g^t_2 : X_j_t to \0,1\ \\ t in \1, ldots, k\ |E[(f_t - E(f_t mid P_i_t otimes P_j_t))g^t_1 g^t_2]|, \\ max_t in \1, ldots, k\ ||f_t - E(f_t mid P'_i_t otimes P'_j_t)||_S^infty le sup_substackh^t_1 : X_i_t to C \\ h^t_2 : X_j_t to C \\ t in \1, ldots, k\^* leftvert E[(f_t - E(f_t mid P'_i_t otimes P'_j_t))h^t_1 h^t_2]rightvert, Thus it suffices to bound the right-hand sides for any specific choice of the tuples of functions \g^t_u\_t,u, respectively \h^t_u\_t,u. Fix such tuples of functions, and consider the partitions of X_i that they collectively induce: \[ Q_i := bigvee_substackt in \1, ldots, k\ \\ i_t = i textnormalPart(g^t_1) vee bigvee_substackt in \1, ldots, k\ \\ j_t = i textnormalPart(g^t_2), Q_i' := bigvee_substackt in \1, ldots, k\ \\ i_t = i textnormalPart(h^t_1) vee bigvee_substackt in \1, ldots, k\ \\ j_t = i textnormalPart(h^t_2). \] Due to the nature of the functions g^t_u and h^t_u, these partitions satisfy the the complexity bounds log |Q_i| ll_k 1 and H(Q_i') ll_k 1. For notational convenience, we also denote R_i := P_i vee Q_i and R_i' := P_i' vee Q_i', which begins to resemble the setting of our abstract energy optimization argument (creflem:energy-optimization). Now for t in \1, ldots, k\, using crefeq:Schatten-infty and the fact that the function (x_1, x_2) mapsto g_1^i,j(x_1) g_2^i,j(x_2) is (R_i_t otimes R_j_t)-measurable, we can write \[ leftvert E[(f_t - E(f_t mid P_i_t otimes P_j_t))g^t_1 g^t_2]rightvert &= leftvert E[(E(f_t mid R_i_t otimes R_j_t) - E(f_t mid P_i_t otimes P_j_t)) g^t_1 g^t_2]rightvert \\ &le ||E(f_t mid R_i_t otimes R_j_t) - E(f_t mid P_i_t otimes P_j_t)||_S^infty cdot ||g_1^t||_L^2 cdot ||g_2^t||_L^2 \\ &ll ||E(f_t mid R_i_t otimes R_j_t) - E(f_t mid P_i_t otimes P_j_t)||_S^infty, \] and similarly, \[ leftvert E[(f_t - E(f_t mid P'_i_t otimes P'_j_t))h^t_1 h^t_2]rightvert ll ||E(f_t mid R'_i_t otimes R'_j_t) - E(f_t mid P'_i_t otimes P'_j_t)||_S^infty. \] Putting things together, to obtain the desired uniformity norm bounds in crefeq:cut-norm-bound,eq:spec-norm-bound, it suffices to have max_t ||E(f_t mid R_i_t otimes R_j_t) - E(f_t mid P_i_t otimes P_j_t)||_S^infty le varepsilon max_t ||f_t||_S^q, \\ max_t ||E(f_t mid R'_i_t otimes R'_j_t) - E(f_t mid P'_i_t otimes P'_j_t)||_S^infty le varepsilon max_t ||f_t||_S^q. We will first present the argument for crefeq:first-supremum, and then mention what changes for crefeq:second-supremum. By creflem:energy-increment for ell := max(lceil log_2 q rceil, 1) ge log_2 q, for each t we have ||E(f_t mid R_i_t otimes R_j_t) - E(f_t mid P_i_t otimes P_j_t))||_S^infty &le (E_f_t,ell(R_i_t) - E_f_t,ell(P_i_t))^1/2^ell \\ &+ (E_f_t^T,ell(R_j_t) - E_f_t^T,ell(P_j_t))^1/2^ell, where all energies are bounded by E_f_t,ell = ||f_t||_S^2^ell^2^ell le ||f_t||_S^q^2^ell le ||f_t||_S^q_t^2^ell. We are finally ready to choose P_i by applying the energy optimization argument in creflem:energy-optimization, once for each i in \1, ldots, m\, to the set Omega = X_i, in the search space P of all partitions of X_i, with the complexity function log |cdot|, cvarepsilon^2^ell in place of varepsilon (for some c > 0 to be chosen shortly), and with the energy function \[ E_i(P_i) := sum_substackt in \1, ldots, k\ \\ i_t = i E_f_t,ell(P_i) + sum_substackt in \1, ldots, k\ \\ j_t = i E_f_t^T,ell(P_i). \] Recalling the notation M := max_t ||f_t||_S^q_t, note that the energy function E_i is nonnegative and bounded above by \[ sum_substackt in \1, ldots, k\ \\ i_t = i E_f_t,ell + sum_substackt in \1, ldots, k\ \\ j_t = i E_f_t^T,ell le sum_substackt in \1, ldots, k\ \\ i_t = i ||f_t||_S^q_t^2^ell + sum_substackt in \1, ldots, k\ \\ j_t = i ||f_t||_S^q_t^2^ell le 2k M^2^ell. \] Thus the resulting P_i satisfy \[ log |P_i| ll frac1cvarepsilon^2^ell ll_c frac1varepsilon^alpha(q,infty) \] and, due to the conclusion of creflem:energy-optimization, crefeq:joint-partitions and crefeq:complexity-bounds, \[ E_i(R_i) - E_i(P_i) ll_k cvarepsilon^2^ell cdot 2k M^2^ell cdot log |Q_i| ll_k c (varepsilon M)^2^ell. \] Choosing c = c(k,q) > 0 small enough in terms of k and ell = ell(q), we conclude that \[ sum_substackt in \1, ldots, k\ \\ i_t = i (E_f_t,ell(R_i) - E_f_t,ell(P_i)) + sum_substackt in \1, ldots, k\ \\ j_t = i (E_f_t^T,ell(R_i) - E_f_t^T,ell(P_i)) le left(fracvarepsilon M2right)^2^ell, \] where each term in the two sums is nonnegative. Putting this together with crefeq:final-energy-bound, we obtain \[ ||E(f_t mid R_i_t otimes R_j_t) - E(f_t mid P_i_t otimes P_j_t))||_S^infty le 2^-1 varepsilon M + 2^-1 varepsilon M = varepsilon M, \] and taking a maximum over t in \1, ldots, k\ yields the desired bound in crefeq:first-supremum. To establish crefeq:second-supremum, we choose the partitions P_i' via creflem:energy-optimization in the same way, except that we use the complexity function H(cdot) instead of log |cdot|. This yields \[ H(P_i') ll_c frac1varepsilon^alpha(q,infty) and E_i(R_i') - E_i(P_i') ll_k cvarepsilon^2^ell cdot 2k M^2^ell cdot H(Q_i'), \] and choosing a suitable constant c = c(k, q) is now possible due to the entropy bound in crefeq:complexity-bounds.
nodes.raw_latex:
We first note that it suffices to consider the case when all $r_t = \infty$, since Schatten norms can be interpolated. Indeed, assuming that \cref{eq:spec-norm-bound} holds when all $r_t = \infty$, one can apply it for $2^{1/(1-\frac{r}{q})}\varepsilon^{1/(1-\frac{q}{r})}$ in place of $\varepsilon$ (for any given $r \in (q, \infty)$); this yields partitions $\mathcal{P}'_i$ with
\[
    \max_i \mathbf{H}(\mathcal{P}'_i) \ll_q \frac{1}{2^{\alpha(q,\infty)/(1-\frac{r}{q})}\varepsilon^{\alpha(q,\infty)/(1 - \frac{q}{r})}}
    \ll_{q,r}
    \frac{1}{\varepsilon^{\alpha(q,r)}},
\]
such that
\[
    \max_t ||f_t - \mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{P}'_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{P}'_{j_t})||_{S^\infty} \le 2^{1/(1-\frac{r}{q})} \varepsilon^{1/(1-\frac{q}{r})} \max_t ||f_t||_{S^{q_t}}.
\]
But then, given any values $r_t \in (q_t, \infty]$ and setting $r := q \min_t(r_t/q_t)$, \cref{lem:Schatten-norms-functions} implies that if $M := \max_t ||f_t||_{S^{q_t}}$, then for each $t \in \{1, \ldots, k\}$ one has
\[
\begin{aligned}
    &||f_t - \mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{P}'_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{P}'_{j_t})||_{S^{r_t}} 
    \\
    &\le
    ||f_t - \mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{P}'_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{P}'_{j_t})||_{S^{q_t}}^{q_t/r_t} \cdot ||f_t - \mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{P}'_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{P}'_{j_t})||_{S^\infty}^{1 - q_t/r_t}
    \\
    &\le 
    \left(||f_t||_{S^{q_t}} + ||\mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{P}'_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{P}'_{j_t})||_{S^{q_t}}\right)^{q_t/r_t} \cdot \left(2^{1/(1-\frac{r}{q})}\varepsilon^{1/(1-\frac{q}{r})} M\right)^{1 - q_t/r_t}
    \\
    &\le 
    \left(2M\right)^{q_t/r_t} \cdot 2^{-q_t/r_t}\varepsilon M^{1 - q_t/r_t}
    \\
    &=
    \varepsilon M.
\end{aligned}
\]


After this reduction, it remains to find partitions $\mathcal{P}_i$ which satisfy \cref{eq:cut-norm-bound}, and $\mathcal{P}_i'$ which satisfy \cref{eq:spec-norm-bound} for $r = r_t = \infty$. For now, fix some partitions $\mathcal{P}_i$ and $\mathcal{P}_i'$ of $X_i$, which will be chosen later via the abstract energy optimization argument in \cref{lem:energy-optimization}; it will take some work to explain how exactly this optimization argument will be applied. By \cref{eq:cut} and \cref{lem:modify-spectral}, we can express the uniformity norms of interest (for $t \in \{1, \ldots, k\}$) as
\begin{gather*}
    ||f_t - \mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{P}_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{P}_{j_t})||_{\substack{ \\ \square}} = \sup_{\substack{g_1 : X_{i_t} \to \{0,1\} \\ g_2 : X_{j_t} \to \{0,1\}}} |\mathbf{E}_{x_1,x_2}[(f_t - \mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{P}_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{P}_{j_t}))(x_1,x_2)g_1(x_1)g_2(x_2)]|,
    \\
    ||f_t - \mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{P}'_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{P}'_{j_t})||_{S^\infty} \le \sup_{\substack{h_1 : X_{i_t} \to \mathbf{C} \\ h_2 : X_{j_t} \to \mathbf{C}}}^* \left\vert \mathbf{E}_{x_1,x_2}[(f_t - \mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{P}'_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{P}'_{j_t}))(x_1,x_2)h_1(x_1)h_2(x_2)]\right\vert,
\end{gather*}
where $x_1$ is sampled from $(X_{i_t}, \mathbf{P}_{i_t})$, $x_2$ is sampled from $(X_{j_t}, \mathbf{P}_{j_t})$, and $\sup_{h_1,h_2}^*$ has the same meaning as in \cref{lem:modify-spectral}.
In particular, all functions involved in both suprema have $||g_u||_{L^2} \ll 1$ and $||h_u||_{L^2} \ll 1$, while each $g_u$ in the first supremum takes at most two values, and each $h_u$ in the second supremum has $\mathbf{H}(h_u) \ll 1$ (for $u \in \{1, 2\}$). Taking a maximum over $t$ and suppressing dependencies on $x_1, x_2$ for notational simplicity, we get
\begin{gather*}
    \max_{t \in \{1, \ldots, k\}} ||f_t - \mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{P}_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{P}_{j_t})||_{\substack{ \\ \square}} = \sup_{\substack{g^t_1 : X_{i_t} \to \{0,1\} \\ g^t_2 : X_{j_t} \to \{0,1\} \\ t \in \{1, \ldots, k\}}} |\mathbf{E}[(f_t - \mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{P}_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{P}_{j_t}))g^t_1 g^t_2]|,
    \\
    \max_{t \in \{1, \ldots, k\}} ||f_t - \mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{P}'_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{P}'_{j_t})||_{S^\infty} \le \sup_{\substack{h^t_1 : X_{i_t} \to \mathbf{C} \\ h^t_2 : X_{j_t} \to \mathbf{C} \\ t \in \{1, \ldots, k\}}}^* \left\vert \mathbf{E}[(f_t - \mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{P}'_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{P}'_{j_t}))h^t_1 h^t_2]\right\vert,
\end{gather*}
Thus it suffices to bound the right-hand sides for any specific choice of the tuples of functions $\{g^t_u\}_{t,u}$, respectively $\{h^t_u\}_{t,u}$. Fix such tuples of functions, and consider the partitions of $X_i$ that they collectively induce:
\[
    \mathcal{Q}_i := \bigvee_{\substack{t \in \{1, \ldots, k\} \\ i_t = i}} \textnormal{Part}(g^t_1) \vee 
    \bigvee_{\substack{t \in \{1, \ldots, k\} \\ j_t = i}} \textnormal{Part}(g^t_2),
    \qquad\quad
    \mathcal{Q}_i' := \bigvee_{\substack{t \in \{1, \ldots, k\} \\ i_t = i}} \textnormal{Part}(h^t_1) \vee 
    \bigvee_{\substack{t \in \{1, \ldots, k\} \\ j_t = i}} \textnormal{Part}(h^t_2).
\] 
Due to the nature of the functions $g^t_u$ and $h^t_u$, these partitions satisfy the the complexity bounds
\begin{equation}\label{eq:complexity-bounds}
    \log |\mathcal{Q}_i| \ll_k 1 \qquad\quad \text{and} \qquad\quad 
    \mathbf{H}(\mathcal{Q}_i') \ll_k 1.
\end{equation}
For notational convenience, we also denote
\begin{equation}\label{eq:joint-partitions}
    \mathcal{R}_i := \mathcal{P}_i \vee \mathcal{Q}_i \qquad\quad \text{and} \qquad\quad 
    \mathcal{R}_i' := \mathcal{P}_i' \vee \mathcal{Q}_i',
\end{equation}
which begins to resemble the setting of our abstract energy optimization argument (\cref{lem:energy-optimization}). Now for $t \in \{1, \ldots, k\}$, using \cref{eq:Schatten-infty} and the fact that the function $(x_1, x_2) \mapsto g_1^{i,j}(x_1) g_2^{i,j}(x_2)$ is $(\mathcal{R}_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{R}_{j_t})$-measurable, we can write
\[
\begin{aligned}
    \left\vert \mathbf{E}[(f_t - \mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{P}_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{P}_{j_t}))g^t_1 g^t_2]\right\vert
    &=
    \left\vert \mathbf{E}[(\mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{R}_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{R}_{j_t}) - \mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{P}_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{P}_{j_t})) g^t_1 g^t_2]\right\vert
    \\
    &\le
    ||\mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{R}_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{R}_{j_t}) - \mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{P}_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{P}_{j_t})||_{S^\infty} \cdot ||g_1^t||_{L^2} \cdot ||g_2^t||_{L^2} 
    \\
    &\ll
    ||\mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{R}_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{R}_{j_t}) - \mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{P}_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{P}_{j_t})||_{S^\infty},
\end{aligned}
\]
and similarly,
\[
    \left\vert \mathbf{E}[(f_t - \mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{P}'_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{P}'_{j_t}))h^t_1 h^t_2]\right\vert \ll
    ||\mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{R}'_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{R}'_{j_t}) - \mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{P}'_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{P}'_{j_t})||_{S^\infty}.
\]
Putting things together, to obtain the desired uniformity norm bounds in \cref{eq:cut-norm-bound,eq:spec-norm-bound}, it suffices to have
\begin{gather}
    \max_t ||\mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{R}_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{R}_{j_t}) - \mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{P}_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{P}_{j_t})||_{S^\infty} \le \varepsilon \max_t ||f_t||_{S^q}, \label{eq:first-supremum}
    \\
    \max_t ||\mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{R}'_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{R}'_{j_t}) - \mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{P}'_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{P}'_{j_t})||_{S^\infty} \le \varepsilon \max_t ||f_t||_{S^q}.
    \label{eq:second-supremum}
\end{gather}

We will first present the argument for \cref{eq:first-supremum}, and then mention what changes for \cref{eq:second-supremum}. By \cref{lem:energy-increment} for $\ell := \max(\lceil \log_2 q \rceil, 1) \ge \log_2 q$, for each $t$ we have
\begin{equation} \label{eq:final-energy-bound}
\begin{aligned}
    ||\mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{R}_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{R}_{j_t}) - \mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{P}_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{P}_{j_t}))||_{S^\infty}
    &\le 
    (\mathcal{E}_{f_t,\ell}(\mathcal{R}_{i_t}) - \mathcal{E}_{f_t,\ell}(\mathcal{P}_{i_t}))^{1/2^\ell} 
    \\
    &+ 
    (\mathcal{E}_{f_t^T,\ell}(\mathcal{R}_{j_t}) - \mathcal{E}_{f_t^T,\ell}(\mathcal{P}_{j_t}))^{1/2^\ell},
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where all energies are bounded by $\mathcal{E}_{f_t,\ell} = ||f_t||_{S^{2^\ell}}^{2^\ell} \le ||f_t||_{S^q}^{2^\ell} \le ||f_t||_{S^{q_t}}^{2^\ell}$. We are finally ready to choose $\mathcal{P}_i$ by applying the energy optimization argument in \cref{lem:energy-optimization}, once for each $i \in \{1, \ldots, m\}$, to the set $\Omega = X_i$, in the search space $\mathscr{P}$ of all partitions of $X_i$, with the complexity function $\log |\cdot|$, $c\varepsilon^{2^\ell}$ in place of $\varepsilon$ (for some $c > 0$ to be chosen shortly), and with the energy function
\[
    \mathcal{E}_i(\mathcal{P}_i) := \sum_{\substack{t \in \{1, \ldots, k\} \\ i_t = i}} \mathcal{E}_{f_t,\ell}(\mathcal{P}_i) + \sum_{\substack{t \in \{1, \ldots, k\} \\ j_t = i}} \mathcal{E}_{f_t^T,\ell}(\mathcal{P}_i).
\]
Recalling the notation $M := \max_t ||f_t||_{S^{q_t}}$, note that the energy function $\mathcal{E}_i$ is nonnegative and bounded above by
\[
    \sum_{\substack{t \in \{1, \ldots, k\} \\ i_t = i}} \mathcal{E}_{f_t,\ell} + 
    \sum_{\substack{t \in \{1, \ldots, k\} \\ j_t = i}} \mathcal{E}_{f_t^T,\ell} 
    \le 
    \sum_{\substack{t \in \{1, \ldots, k\} \\ i_t = i}} ||f_t||_{S^{q_t}}^{2^\ell} + 
    \sum_{\substack{t \in \{1, \ldots, k\} \\ j_t = i}} ||f_t||_{S^{q_t}}^{2^\ell} 
    \le 2k 
    M^{2^\ell}.
\]
Thus the resulting $\mathcal{P}_i$ satisfy 
\[
    \log |\mathcal{P}_i| \ll \frac{1}{c\varepsilon^{2^\ell}} \ll_c \frac{1}{\varepsilon^{\alpha(q,\infty)}}
\]
and, due to the conclusion of \cref{lem:energy-optimization}, \cref{eq:joint-partitions} and \cref{eq:complexity-bounds},
\[
    \mathcal{E}_i(\mathcal{R}_i) - \mathcal{E}_i(\mathcal{P}_i)
    \ll_k c\varepsilon^{2^\ell} \cdot 2k M^{2^\ell} \cdot  \log |\mathcal{Q}_i|
    \ll_k 
    c (\varepsilon M)^{2^\ell}.
\]
Choosing $c = c(k,q) > 0$ small enough in terms of $k$ and $\ell = \ell(q)$, we conclude that
\[
    \sum_{\substack{t \in \{1, \ldots, k\} \\ i_t = i}} (\mathcal{E}_{f_t,\ell}(\mathcal{R}_i) -
    \mathcal{E}_{f_t,\ell}(\mathcal{P}_i)) 
    + 
    \sum_{\substack{t \in \{1, \ldots, k\} \\ j_t = i}} (\mathcal{E}_{f_t^T,\ell}(\mathcal{R}_i) -
    \mathcal{E}_{f_t^T,\ell}(\mathcal{P}_i))
    \le \left(\frac{\varepsilon M}{2}\right)^{2^\ell},
\]
where each term in the two sums is nonnegative.
Putting this together with \cref{eq:final-energy-bound}, we obtain
\[
    ||\mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{R}_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{R}_{j_t}) - \mathbf{E}(f_t \mid \mathcal{P}_{i_t} \otimes \mathcal{P}_{j_t}))||_{S^\infty} \le 
    2^{-1} \varepsilon M + 2^{-1} \varepsilon M
    =
    \varepsilon M,
\]
and taking a maximum over $t \in \{1, \ldots, k\}$ yields the desired bound in \cref{eq:first-supremum}. 

To establish \cref{eq:second-supremum}, we choose the partitions $\mathcal{P}_i'$ via \cref{lem:energy-optimization} in the same way, except that we use the complexity function $\mathbf{H}(\cdot)$ instead of $\log |\cdot|$. This yields
\[
    \mathbf{H}(\mathcal{P}_i') \ll_c \frac{1}{\varepsilon^{\alpha(q,\infty)}}
    \qquad \quad 
    \text{and} 
    \qquad \quad 
    \mathcal{E}_i(\mathcal{R}_i') - \mathcal{E}_i(\mathcal{P}_i')
    \ll_k c\varepsilon^{2^\ell} \cdot 2k M^{2^\ell} \cdot  \mathbf{H}(\mathcal{Q}_i'),
\]
and choosing a suitable constant $c = c(k, q)$ is now possible due to the entropy bound in  \cref{eq:complexity-bounds}.

nodes.statement: One can also give a constructive proof of a statement like crefthm:regularity using singular value decomposition (related to the spectral methods of Frieze and Kannan ), at the expense of inserting cutoffs of the form mathbbm1_R_i^c times R_j^c in the uniformity norms, for some small exceptional sets R_i. Such cutoffs are compatible with our methods, and can eliminate the need to use entropy as a measure of complexity. We chose the method of proof above partly since we find it cleaner, and partly since the generalized L^2 energies from crefdef:generalized-L2-energy might find other applications (in particular, they may have higher-order combinatorial analogues, applicable in the setting of hypergraphs).

Let $(X_i, \mathbf{P}_i)$ be finite probability spaces and $f_i, \widetilde{f}_i : X_i \times X_{i+1} \to [0, \infty)$ be functions satisfying $||f_i||_{L^\infty} \le C$, $||\widetilde{f}_i||_{L^\infty} \le C$, and $||f_i - \widetilde{f}_i||_{\substack{ \\ \square}} \le \varepsilon$, for $i \in \mathbf{Z}/k\mathbf{Z}$.     -
    \mathbf{E}_{x_1, \ldots, x_k} \prod_{i=1}^k \widetilde{f}_{i}(x_i,x_{i+1}) 
    \right\vert
    \le k C^{k-1}
    \varepsilon.
\]

Then \[ leftvert E_x_1, ldots, x_k prod_i=1^k f_i(x_i,x_i+1) - E_x_1, ldots, x_k prod_i=1^k widetildef_i(x_i,x_i+1) rightvert le k C^k-1 varepsilon. \]
assumptions: Let k in Z_ge 2, q_1, ldots, q_k in [1, infty), and r_1, ldots, r_k in (1, infty] be such that for each i in Z/kZ, \[ frac1r_i + sum_j neq i frac1q_j ge 1.

\] Also, let varepsilon, C > 0, (X_i, P_i) be finite probability spaces, and f_i, widetildef_i : X_i times X_i+1 to C be functions satisfying ||f_i||_S^q_i le C, ||widetildef_i||_S^q_i le C, and ||f_i - widetildef_i||_S^r_i le varepsilon, for i in Z/kZ.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{lem:counting}
Let $k \in \mathbf{Z}_{\ge 2}$, $q_1, \ldots, q_k \in [1, \infty)$, and $r_1, \ldots, r_k \in (1, \infty]$ be such that for each $i \in \mathbf{Z}/k\mathbf{Z}$,
\[
    \frac{1}{r_i} + \sum_{j \neq i} \frac{1}{q_j} \ge 1.
\]
Also, let $\varepsilon, C > 0$, $(X_i, \mathbf{P}_i)$ be finite probability spaces, and $f_{i}, \widetilde{f}_{i} : X_i \times X_{i+1} \to \mathbf{C}$ be functions satisfying $||f_{i}||_{S^{q_i}} \le C$, $||\widetilde{f}_{i}||_{S^{q_i}} \le C$, and $||f_{i} - \widetilde{f}_{i}||_{S^{r_i}} \le \varepsilon$, for $i \in \mathbf{Z}/k\mathbf{Z}$. Then
\[
    \left\vert \mathbf{E}_{x_1, \ldots, x_k} \prod_{i=1}^k f_{i}(x_i,x_{i+1})
    -
    \mathbf{E}_{x_1, \ldots, x_k} \prod_{i=1}^k \widetilde{f}_{i}(x_i,x_{i+1}) 
    \right\vert
    \le k C^{k-1}
    \varepsilon.
\]

For any graph $F \in \{C_k : k \ge 5\} \cup \{P_k : k \ge 1\}$ and any $\epsilon, C > 0$, there exists $\delta > 0$ such that the following holds. Let $G$ be an $n$-vertex graph with $\textnormal{Inj}(C_4, G) \le Cn^2$, and $H \in [0, \infty)^{V(G) \times V(G)}$ be a symmetric matrix with $\textnormal{Tr}(H^4) \le Cn^4$, such that
\[
    \left\vert \frac{\sum_{x,y} \mathbbm{1}_{G}(x,y) a(x)b(y)}{n^{3/2}} - \frac{\sum_{x,y} H(x,y)a(x)b(y)}{n^2} \right\vert \le \delta
    \qquad
    \forall a, b : V(G) \to \mathbf{C},\  ||a||_{2}, ||b||_{2} \le \sqrt{n}.
\]
Then for every family $(A_v)_{v \in V(F)}$ of subsets $A_v \subset V(G)$, one has

    -

    \right\vert

\]

Equip $V(G)$ with the uniform probability measure, and define $f, \widetilde{f} : V(G) \times V(G) \to [0, \infty)$ by $f := \mathbbm{1}_{G}/p$ and $\widetilde{f} := H$, for $p = n^{-1/2}$ (one can in fact use any $p \ge n^{-1/2}$ to obtain a slightly more general result). A short computation of Conlon, Fox, Sudakov and Zhao \cite[p.\ 2389, below $(11)$]{conlon2021regularity} shows that for any $n$-vertex graph $G$, one has
\begin{equation} \label{eq:4-cycle-counts}
    \textnormal{Hom}(C_4, G) 
    \ll n^2 + \textnormal{Inj}(C_4, G),
\end{equation}
with an absolute implied constant. Using \cref{eq:2k-cycles} and our assumption that $\textnormal{Inj}(C_4, G) \le Cn^4$, this yields
\[
    ||f||_{S^4}^4 = \frac{\textnormal{Hom}(C_4, G)}{p^4 n^4}
    \le \frac{C' n^2}{p^4 n^4} = C',
\]
for some constant $C' > 0$ (depending only on $C$). Similarly, $\textnormal{Tr}(H^4) \le Cn^4$ translates to $||\widetilde{f}||_{S^4} \le C^{1/4}$, and the assumed $\delta$-bound involving functions $a, b : V(G) \to \mathbf{C}$ simply states that
\[
    ||f - \widetilde{f}||_{S^\infty} \le \delta,
\]
by \cref{eq:Schatten-infty} (in \cite{conlon2021graphs}, $a$ and $b$ are required to be indicator functions of subsets of $V(G)$, which amounts to the less restrictive cut norm bound $||f - \widetilde{f}||_{\substack{ \\ \square}} \le \delta$). Finally, the desired conclusion translates to
\begin{equation} \label{eq:counting-conclusion-1}
    \left\vert 
    \mathbf{E}_{x_1, \ldots, x_k} \prod_{v \in \mathbf{Z}/k\mathbf{Z}} (f \mathbbm{1}_{A_v \times A_{v+1}})(x_v,x_{v+1})
    -
    \mathbf{E}_{x_1, \ldots, x_k} \prod_{v \in \mathbf{Z}/k\mathbf{Z}} (\widetilde{f} \mathbbm{1}_{A_v \times A_{v+1}})(x_v,x_{v+1})
    \right\vert
    \le \epsilon,
\end{equation}
when $F = C_k$ is a $k$-cycle with $k \ge 5$ (and $V(F) = \mathbf{Z}/k\mathbf{Z}$), respectively
\begin{equation} \label{eq:counting-conclusion-2}
    \left\vert 
    \mathbf{E}_{x_1, \ldots, x_k} \prod_{v = 1}^{k-1} (f \mathbbm{1}_{A_v \times A_{v+1}})(x_v,x_{v+1})
    -
    \mathbf{E}_{x_1, \ldots, x_k} \prod_{v = 1}^{k-1} (\widetilde{f} \mathbbm{1}_{A_v \times A_{v+1}})(x_v,x_{v+1})
    \right\vert
    \le \epsilon,
\end{equation}
when $F = P_{k-1}$ is a $(k-1)$-path with $k \ge 2$ (and vertex set $V(F) = \{1, \ldots, k\}$). Letting $f_v := f \mathbbm{1}_{A_v \times A_{v+1}}$ and $\widetilde{f}_v := \widetilde{f} \mathbbm{1}_{A_v \times A_{v+1}}$, we still have $||f_v||_{S^4}, ||\widetilde{f}_v||_{S^4} \ll_C 1$ and $||f_v - \widetilde{f}_v||_{S^\infty} \le \delta$ for each $v$, by \cref{lem:Schatten-norms-functions}. 

Thus \cref{eq:counting-conclusion-1} follows immediately from \cref{lem:counting}, by picking a small enough $\delta$ and noting that $\frac{1}{\infty} + \sum_{v=1}^{k-1} \frac{1}{4} \ge 1$. Similarly, \cref{eq:counting-conclusion-2} follows from \cref{lem:counting}, by inserting constant functions $f_k = \widetilde{f}_k := \mathbbm{1}_{V(G)}$ with $||f_k||_{S^1} = ||\widetilde{f}_k||_{S^1} = 1$ (by \cref{lem:Schatten-norms-functions}), and noting that $\frac{1}{\infty} + \sum_{v=1}^{k-2} \frac{1}{4} + 1 \ge 1$.

Now let $A_1, \ldots, A_k$ denote some (not necessarily distinct) parts of $\mathcal{P}$, which have at least $k(k+1)$ vertices (i.e., $A_1, \ldots, A_k \subset R^c$). Consider the expectation
\[
    \mathbf{E}_{x_1, \ldots, x_k} f(x_1,\ldots,x_k) \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbbm{1}_{X^{(i)} \cap A_i}(x_i),
\]
where $x_1, \ldots, x_k$ still range over $X$, although only the values $(x_1, \ldots, x_k) \in A_1 \times \cdots \times A_k$ are relevant. Note that for these values, $f(x_1,\ldots,x_k)$ is equal to some nonnegative constant $c(A_1,\ldots,A_k)$. Moreover, by the construction of $X^{(i)}$, the intersection $X^{(i)} \cap A_i$ contains at least 
\[
    \left\lfloor \frac{|A_i|}{k} \right\rfloor \ge \frac{|A_i| - k}{k} \ge \frac{|A_i|}{k+1}
\]
vertices, and thus $\mathbf{E}_{x_i} \mathbbm{1}_{X^{(i)} \cap A_i}(x_i) \ge \frac{1}{k+1} \mathbf{E}_{x_i} \mathbbm{1}_{A_i}(x_i)$ (since we are using the uniform probability distribution on $X$). It follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{E}_{x_1,\ldots,x_k} f(x_1,\ldots,x_k) \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbbm{1}_{X^{(i)} \cap A_i}(x_i)
    &= 
    c(A_1, \ldots, A_k) \mathbf{E}_{x_1,\ldots,x_k} \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbbm{1}_{X^{(i)} \cap A_i}(x_i)
    \\ 
    &\ge 
    \frac{1}{(k+1)^k} c(A_1, \ldots, A_k) \mathbf{E}_{x_1,\ldots,x_k} \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbbm{1}_{A_i}(x_i)
    \\

\end{aligned}
\]
and summing over all choices of $A_1 \times \cdots \times A_k$, we conclude that
\[
\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{E}_{x_1,\ldots,x_k} f(x_1,\ldots,x_k) \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbbm{1}_{R^c}(x_i)
    &\ll_k

    \\

\label{prop:reduction-to-structure}
For any $k \in \mathbf{Z}_{\ge 2}$ and $q_1, \ldots, q_k \in [1, \infty)$ with $\sum_i \frac{1}{q_i} > 1$, and any $\varepsilon, C > 0$, there exists $\tau > 0$ such that the following hold. Let $(X_i, \mathbf{P}_i)$ be finite probability spaces, and $f_{i} : X_i \times X_{i+1} \to \mathbf{C}$ satisfy $||f_{i}||_{S^{q_i}} \le C$, for $i \in \mathbf{Z}/k\mathbf{Z}$.
\begin{itemize}
    \item[$(i)$.] There exist partitions $\mathcal{P}_i'$ of $X_i$ with $\mathbf{H}(\mathcal{P}_i') = O_{\varepsilon,k,q_1, \ldots, q_k,C}(1)$, such that
    \[
        \left\vert \mathbf{E}_{x_1, \ldots, x_k} \prod_{i=1}^k f_{i}(x_i,x_{i+1})
        -
        \mathbf{E}_{x_1, \ldots, x_k} \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbf{E}(f_{i} \mid \mathcal{P}'_i \otimes \mathcal{P}'_{i+1})(x_i,x_{i+1}) 
        \right\vert
        \le
        \varepsilon.
    \]
    \item[$(ii)$.] If all $f_{i}$ take values in $[0, \infty)$, then there exist partitions $\mathcal{P}_i = \{R_i, A_{i,1}, A_{i,2}, \ldots\}$ of $X_i$, with $\mathbf{P}_i(R_i) \le \varepsilon^2$ and $\mathbf{P}(A_{i,j}) \ge \tau$ for all $i, j$, such that
    \[
        \mathbf{E}_{x_1, \ldots, x_k} \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbf{E}(f_{i} \mid \mathcal{P}_i \otimes \mathcal{P}_{i+1})(x_i, x_{i+1})\mathbbm{1}_{R_i^c}(x_i) \le \varepsilon + \mathbf{E}_{x_1, \ldots, x_k} \prod_{i=1}^k f_{i}(x_i,x_{i+1}).
    \]
    \item[$(iii)$.] If additionally all spaces $(X_i, \mathbf{P}_i) = (X, \mathbf{P})$ are equal and $\mathbf{P}$ is the uniform probability distribution, and $|X|$ is sufficiently large in terms of $\varepsilon,k,q_1, \ldots, q_k, C$, then in part (ii) one can take all $\mathcal{P}_i = \mathcal{P}$ and $R_i = R$ to be equal, and also conclude the stronger bound
    \[
        \mathbf{E}_{x_1, \ldots, x_k} \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbf{E}(f_{i} \mid \mathcal{P} \otimes \mathcal{P})(x_i,x_{i+1}) \mathbbm{1}_{R^c}(x_i) 
        \ll_k
        \varepsilon + \mathbf{E}_{x_1, \ldots, x_k} \mathbbm{1}_{x_1,\ldots,x_k \textnormal{ distinct}}\prod_{i=1}^k f_{i}(x_i,x_{i+1}).
    \]
\end{itemize}

Assume without loss of generality that $\varepsilon/(kC^k) < 1$ (by making $\varepsilon$ smaller if necessary).
To prove $(i)$, apply \cref{thm:regularity} for the functions $f_{i}$, and with
\begin{equation} \label{eq:r-choice}
\begin{aligned}
    r_i := q_i + q_i^2\left(\sum_j \frac{1}{q_j}-1\right) > q_i
    \qquad 
    &\Rightarrow 
    \qquad 
    \frac{1}{q_i} - \frac{1}{r_i} \le \frac{r_i - q_i}{q_i^2} = \sum_j \frac{1}{q_j}-1
    \\
    &\Rightarrow 
    \qquad 
    \frac{1}{r_i} + \sum_{j \neq i} \frac{1}{q_j} \ge 1.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
This produces partitions $\mathcal{P}_i'$ of $X_i$ such that $\mathbf{H}(\mathcal{P}_i') = O_{\varepsilon,k,q_1, \ldots, q_k,C}(1)$ and 
\[
    \max_i ||f_{i} - \mathbf{E}(f_{i} \mid \mathcal{P}_i' \otimes \mathcal{P}_{i+1}')||_{S^{r_i}} \le \frac{\varepsilon}{kC^k} \max_i ||f_{i}||_{S^{q_i}} \le \frac{\varepsilon}{kC^{k-1}}.
\]
The conclusion now follows from our counting lemma (\cref{lem:counting}).

For $(ii)$, consider the partitions $\mathcal{P}_i'$ from $(i)$, and let $\mathcal{P}_i$ be obtained from $\mathcal{P}'_i$ by combining all parts with probability less than $\tau$ into one part $R_i$ (for some parameter $\tau \in (0, 1)$ to be chosen shortly). Then, if $p_1, p_2, \ldots$ denote the probabilities of all parts of $\mathcal{P}'_i$, we have 
\begin{equation} \label{eq:entropy-bound}
\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{P}_i(R_i) = \sum_{p_n < \tau} p_n 
    &=
    \frac{1}{\log (1/\tau)} \sum_{p_n < \tau} p_n \log \frac{1}{\tau}
    \\
    &\le 
    \frac{1}{\log (1/\tau)} \sum_{n} p_n \log \frac{1}{p_n}
    =
    \frac{\mathbf{H}(\mathcal{P}_i')}{\log(1/\tau)} = O_{\varepsilon,k,q,C}\left(\frac{1}{\log(1/\tau)} \right).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
We can thus pick $\tau = \tau(\varepsilon,k,q_1, \ldots, q_k,C)$ small enough so that $\mathbf{P}_i(R_{i}) \le \varepsilon^2$ (uniformly in $i$). Since the functions $\mathbf{E}(f_{i} \mid \mathcal{P}_i' \otimes \mathcal{P}_{i+1}')$ and $\mathbf{E}(f_{i} \mid \mathcal{P}_i \otimes \mathcal{P}_{i+1})$ are equal inside $R_i^c \times R_{i+1}^c$, we conclude (using $(i)$) that
\[
\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{E}_{x_1, \ldots, x_k} \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbf{E}(f_{i} \mid \mathcal{P}_i \otimes \mathcal{P}_{i+1})\mathbbm{1}_{R_{i}^c}(x_i) 
    &\le
    \mathbf{E}_{x_1, \ldots, x_k} \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbf{E}(f_{i} \mid \mathcal{P}_i' \otimes \mathcal{P}_{i+1}')(x_i,x_{i+1}) 
    \\
    &\le \varepsilon + \mathbf{E}_{x_1, \ldots, x_k} \prod_{i=1}^k f_{i}(x_i,x_{i+1}).
\end{aligned}
\]

Finally, to prove $(iii)$, we apply \cref{thm:regularity} as before, except that now all vertex sets are equal (so $m = 1$). This produces a partition $\mathcal{P}'$ of $X$ such that $\mathbf{H}(\mathcal{P}') = O_{\varepsilon,k,q_1, \ldots, q_k,C}(1)$ and
\[
    \max_i ||f_{i} - \mathbf{E}(f_{i} \mid \mathcal{P}' \otimes \mathcal{P}')||_{S^{r_i}} \le \frac{\varepsilon}{kC^k} \max_i ||f_{i}||_{S^{q_i}} \le \frac{\varepsilon}{kC^{k-1}}.
\]
We repeat the construction of $\mathcal{P}_i$ and $R_i$ from part $(ii)$ (except that now there is only one partition), to obtain a partition $\mathcal{P}$ with $|\mathcal{P}| = O_{\varepsilon,k,q_1, \ldots, q_k,C}(1)$, and a $\mathcal{P}$-measurable set $R$ with $\mathbf{P}(R) \le \varepsilon^2$, which is the union of all parts of $\mathcal{P}'$ with probability less than $\tau = \tau(\varepsilon,k,q_1,\ldots,q_k,C)$.

Now assume that $|X|$ is large enough so that $k(k+1)/|X| < \tau$, and apply \cref{lem:distinct-vertices} for the partition $\mathcal{P}'$ and the $(\bigotimes_{i=1}^k \mathcal{P}')$-measurable function 
\[
    f(x_1,\ldots,x_k) := \prod_{i=1}^k\mathbf{E}(f_{i} \mid \mathcal{P}' \otimes \mathcal{P}')(x_i, x_{i+1}),
\]
to obtain a partition of $X$ into $k$ disjoint parts $X^{(1)}, \ldots, X^{(k)}$, such that
\[
    \mathbf{E}_{x_1,\ldots,x_k} \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbf{E}(f_{i} \mid \mathcal{P}' \otimes \mathcal{P}')(x_i, x_{i+1}) \mathbbm{1}_{R^c}(x_i) \ll_k 
    \mathbf{E}_{x_1,\ldots,x_k} \prod_{i=1}^k
    \mathbf{E}(f_{i} \mid \mathcal{P}' \otimes \mathcal{P}')(x_i, x_{i+1}) \mathbbm{1}_{X^{(i)}}(x_i).
\]
Denoting
\[
\begin{aligned}
    g_{i}(x_i, x_{i+1}) &:= f_{i}(x_i,x_{i+1}) \mathbbm{1}_{X^{(i)}}(x_i), \\
    \widetilde{g}_{i}(x_i, x_{i+1}) &:= \mathbf{E}(f_{i} \mid \mathcal{P}' \otimes \mathcal{P}')(x_i,x_{i+1}) \mathbbm{1}_{X^{(i)}}(x_i),
\end{aligned} 
\]
\cref{lem:Schatten-norms-functions} implies that
\[
    ||g_{i} - \widetilde{g}_{i}||_{S^{r_i}} \le ||f_{i} - \mathbf{E}(f_{i} \mid \mathcal{P}' \otimes \mathcal{P}')||_{S^{r_i}} \le \frac{\varepsilon}{kC^{k-1}}.
\]
We can thus apply our counting lemma, \cref{lem:counting}, for the spaces $X_i = X$ and the functions $g_{i}, \widetilde{g}_{i}$, to obtain
\[
    \left\vert \mathbf{E}_{x_1,\ldots,x_k} \prod_{i=1}^k g_{i}(x_i,x_{i+1}) - \mathbf{E}_{x_1,\ldots,x_k} \prod_{i=1}^k \widetilde{g}_{i}(x_i,x_{i+1})\right\vert \le \varepsilon.
\]
The point of splitting $X$ into $k$ parts and inserting the indicator functions $\mathbbm{1}_{X^{(i)}}(x_i)$ was to force the product $\prod_{i=1}^k g_{i}(x_i,x_{i+1})$ to vanish when $x_1, \ldots, x_k$ are not pairwise distinct; it follows that 
\[
    \mathbf{E}_{x_1,\ldots,x_k} \prod_{i=1}^k g_{i}(x_i,x_{i+1}) \le 
    \mathbf{E}_{x_1, \ldots, x_k} \mathbbm{1}_{x_1,\ldots,x_k \text{ distinct}}\prod_{i=1}^k f_{i}(x_i,x_{i+1}),
\]
and thus putting things together, we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{E}_{x_1,\ldots,x_k} \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbf{E}(f_{i} \mid \mathcal{P}' \otimes \mathcal{P}')(x_i, x_{i+1}) \mathbbm{1}_{R^c}(x_i) 
    &\ll_k
    \mathbf{E}_{x_1,\ldots,x_k} \prod_{i=1}^k
    \widetilde{g}_{i}(x_i, x_{i+1}) 
    \\
    &\le
    \varepsilon +
    \mathbf{E}_{x_1,\ldots,x_k} \prod_{i=1}^k
    g_{i}(x_i, x_{i+1}) 
    \\
    &\le
    \varepsilon + \mathbf{E}_{x_1, \ldots, x_k} \mathbbm{1}_{x_1,\ldots,x_k \textnormal{ distinct}}\prod_{i=1}^k f_{i}(x_i,x_{i+1}).
\end{aligned}
\]
But the functions $\mathbf{E}(f_{i} \mid \mathcal{P}' \otimes \mathcal{P}')$ and $\mathbf{E}(f_{i} \mid \mathcal{P} \otimes \mathcal{P})$ are equal inside $R^c \times R^c$, so the same conclusion holds for $\mathcal{P}$ instead of $\mathcal{P}'$.

nodes.statement: To clarify our notation, the implied constants may depend on the fixed parameters, but not on n and p. It is worth noting that a random (Erd\"os--R\'enyi) graph with asymp pn^2 edges has an expected number of asymp p^j n^j+1 P_j's and asymp p^2k n^2k C_2k's, and the conclusion of crefthm:expected-cycles-paths confirms these predictions under relatively mild assumptions. What makes this result nontrivial is the fact that we are counting injective copies of P_j and C_2k; if we counted homomorphic copies instead, the result would be a relatively straight-forward corollary of the fact that paths and even-length cycles are bipartite graphs with Sidorenko's property .

Apply part $(iii)$ of \cref{prop:reduction-to-structure} with $k+1$ in place of $k$, $q_1 = \cdots = q_{k} = q$ and $q_{k+1} = 1$, and the functions $f_{1} = \cdots = f_{k} = f$ and $f_{k+1} = \mathbbm{1}_{X_k \times X_1}$ (recall that $||f_{k+1}||_{S^1} = 1$ by \cref{lem:Schatten-norms-functions}). This produces a partition $\mathcal{P}$ of $X$ and a $\mathcal{P}$-measurable subset $R \subset X$, such that $\mathbf{P}(R) \le \varepsilon^2$ and
\[
    \mathbf{E}_{x_1,\ldots,x_{k+1}} \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbf{E}(f \mid \mathcal{P} \otimes \mathcal{P})(x_i, x_{i+1}) \mathbbm{1}_{R^c}(x_i) \ll_k \varepsilon.
\]
Letting $g := \mathbf{E}(f \mid \mathcal{P} \otimes \mathcal{P}) \mathbbm{1}_{R^c \times R^c}$, we thus have $\mathbf{E}_{x_1,\ldots,x_{k+1}} \prod_{i=1}^k g(x_i, x_{i+1}) \ll_k \varepsilon$. But since $g$ is symmetric and nonnegative, an older result of Blakley and Roy \cite{blakley1965holder} implies that
\[
    \mathbf{E}_{x_1,\ldots,x_{k+1}}
    \prod_{i=1}^k g(x_i, x_{i+1}) 
    \ge 
    \left( \mathbf{E}_{x_1,x_2} g(x_1, x_2) \right)^k.
\]
(Blakley and Roy state their result in the form $\langle u, G^ku \rangle \ge \langle u, Gu \rangle^k$, for any nonnegative symmetric $n \times n$ matrix $G$, and any $u \in \mathbf{R}^n$ with $||u||_{2} = 1$; we can recover the inequality above by letting $n := |X|$, $G := \textnormal{Mat}(g)$, and $u_x := \sqrt{1/|X|}$ for all $x \in X$. This can also be interpreted as the statement that paths satisfy Sidorenko's conjecture \cite{sidorenko1991inequalities}.) 

We thus get $||g||_{L^1} \ll_k \varepsilon^{1/k}$. But $R^c \times R^c$ is $(\mathcal{P} \otimes \mathcal{P})$-measurable, so 
\[
\begin{aligned}
    \varepsilon^{1/k} \gg_k ||g||_{L^1}
    &= ||f \mathbbm{1}_{R^c \times R^c}||_{L^1} 
    \\
    &\ge ||f||_{L^1} - 2||f \mathbbm{1}_{R \times X}||_{L^1}. 
\end{aligned}
\]
Recalling from \cref{eq:Schatten-infty} that 
\[
    ||f \mathbbm{1}_{R \times X}||_{L^1} \le ||f||_{S^\infty} ||\mathbbm{1}_R||_{L^2} ||\mathbbm{1}_X||_{L^2} 
    \le ||f||_{S^q} \sqrt{\mathbf{P}(R)} \le C\varepsilon,
\]
we reach the desired conclusion, $||f||_{L^1} \ll_k \varepsilon^{1/k} + C\varepsilon$.

nodes.statement: Apply crefprop:graphs-transference-free for the same values of j, k, ell, epsilon, C, to obtain some n_0, delta > 0 such that the following contrapositive statement holds. For any n ge n_0 and p > 0, and any n-vertex graph G with ge epsilon p n^2 edges and textnormalHom(C_2ell, G) le C p^2ell n^2ell, one has \[ textnormalInj(P_j, G) > delta p^j n^j+1 and textnormalInj(C_2k, G) > delta p^2k n^2k. \] We wish to find constants alpha, beta (depending on j, k, ell, epsilon, C) such that \[ alpha p^j n^j+1 le textnormalInj(P_j, G) le beta p^j n^j+1 and alpha p^2k n^2k le textnormalInj(C_2k, G) le beta p^2k n^2k, \] and we can already take alpha := 1/delta for the desired lower bounds. For the upper bounds, first note that by crefeq:2k-cycles, the condition textnormalHom(C_2ell, G) le Cp^2ell n^2ell means ||mathbbm1_G/p||_S^2ell le C^1/2ell. Since ||mathbbm1_G/p||_S^2k le ||mathbbm1_G/p||_S^2ell, we get \[ textnormalInj(C_2k, G) le textnormalHom(C_2k, G) = n^2k ||mathbbm1_G||_S^2k^2k le C^k/ell p^2k n^2k. \] Similarly, after fixing an ordering of the vertices of G (and equipping V(G) with the uniform probability measure), one has \[ textnormalInj(P_j,G) le textnormalHom(P_j, G) = sum_v_1, ldots, v_j+1 in V(G) prod_i=1^k mathbbm1_G(v_i, v_i+1) = n^j+1 langle u, textnormalMat(mathbbm1_G)^j u rangle, \] where u in R^n is the constant vector with each entry equal to 1/sqrtn (and thus ||u||_2 = 1). We now have \[ langle u, textnormalMat(mathbbm1_G)^j urangle le leftvert leftvert textnormalMat(mathbbm1_G)^j rightvert rightvert_S^infty = leftvert leftvert textnormalMat(mathbbm1_G) rightvert rightvert_S^infty^j = ||mathbbm1_G||_S^infty^j, \] since the singular values of a self-adjoint matrix are just the absolute values of its eigenvalues (thus the singular values of textnormalMat(mathbbm1_G)^j are the jth powers of the singular values of textnormalMat(mathbbm1_G)). Putting things together, we get \[ textnormalInj(P_j,G) le n^j+1 ||mathbbm1_G||_S^infty^j le n^j+1 ||mathbbm1_G||_S^2ell^j le C^j/2ell p^j n^j+1. \] So we can take beta := max(C^k/ell, C^j/2ell), and our proof is complete.
nodes.raw_latex:
Apply \cref{prop:graphs-transference-free} for the same values of $j, k, \ell, \epsilon, C$, to obtain some $n_0, \delta > 0$ such that the following contrapositive statement holds. For any $n \ge n_0$ and $p > 0$, and any $n$-vertex graph $G$ with $\ge \epsilon p n^2$ edges and $\textnormal{Hom}(C_{2\ell}, G) \le C p^{2\ell} n^{2\ell}$, one has
\[
    \textnormal{Inj}(P_{j}, G) > \delta p^{j} n^{j+1}
    \qquad\qquad 
    \text{and} 
    \qquad\qquad 
    \textnormal{Inj}(C_{2k}, G) > \delta p^{2k} n^{2k}.
\]
We wish to find constants $\alpha, \beta$ (depending on $j, k, \ell, \epsilon, C$) such that
\[
    \alpha p^j n^{j+1} \le \textnormal{Inj}(P_{j}, G) \le \beta p^{j} n^{j+1}
    \qquad\quad \text{and} \qquad\quad 
    \alpha p^{2k} n^{2k} \le \textnormal{Inj}(C_{2k}, G) \le \beta p^{2k} n^{2k},
\]
and we can already take $\alpha := 1/\delta$ for the desired lower bounds. For the upper bounds, first note that by \cref{eq:2k-cycles}, the condition $\textnormal{Hom}(C_{2\ell}, G) \le Cp^{2\ell} n^{2\ell}$ means $||\mathbbm{1}_{G}/p||_{S^{2\ell}} \le C^{1/{2\ell}}$. Since $||\mathbbm{1}_{G}/p||_{S^{2k}} \le ||\mathbbm{1}_{G}/p||_{S^{2\ell}}$, we get
\[
    \textnormal{Inj}(C_{2k}, G) \le \textnormal{Hom}(C_{2k}, G)
    =
    n^{2k} ||\mathbbm{1}_{G}||_{S^{2k}}^{2k}
    \le 
    C^{k/\ell} p^{2k} n^{2k}.
\]
Similarly, after fixing an ordering of the vertices of $G$ (and equipping $V(G)$ with the uniform probability measure), one has
\[
    \textnormal{Inj}(P_{j},G) \le \textnormal{Hom}(P_{j}, G) = 
    \sum_{v_1, \ldots, v_{j+1} \in V(G)} \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbbm{1}_{G}(v_i, v_{i+1})
    =
    n^{j+1} \langle u, \textnormal{Mat}(\mathbbm{1}_{G})^{j} u \rangle,
\]
where $u \in \mathbf{R}^n$ is the constant vector with each entry equal to $1/\sqrt{n}$ (and thus $||u||_{2} = 1$). We now have
\[
    \langle u, \textnormal{Mat}(\mathbbm{1}_{G})^{j} u\rangle
    \le 
    \left\vert \left\vert \textnormal{Mat}(\mathbbm{1}_{G})^{j} \right\vert \right\vert_{S^\infty}
    =
    \left\vert \left\vert \textnormal{Mat}(\mathbbm{1}_{G}) \right\vert \right\vert_{S^\infty}^{j} = 
    ||\mathbbm{1}_{G}||_{S^\infty}^{j},
\]
since the singular values of a self-adjoint matrix are just the absolute values of its eigenvalues (thus the singular values of $\textnormal{Mat}(\mathbbm{1}_G)^j$ are the $j$th powers of the singular values of $\textnormal{Mat}(\mathbbm{1}_G)$). Putting things together, we get
\[
    \textnormal{Inj}(P_j,G) \le n^{j+1} ||\mathbbm{1}_{G}||_{S^\infty}^{j}

Note that 0 le g_i le 1 everywhere, so we can apply the dense removal lemma (crefthm:dense-k-cycle-removal) for the probability spaces (X_i, Sigma(P_i), P_i) and the functions g_i. We finally pick delta = delta(epsilon, K, k) small enough, as given by crefthm:dense-k-cycle-removal, to find (P_i otimes P_i+1)-measurable subsets E_i subset X_i times X_i+1 such that \[ prod_i=1^k mathbbm1_E_i(x_i, x_i+1) = 0 and ||g_i mathbbm1_E_i^c||_L^1 le fracepsilon16K, \] for all x_1, ldots, x_k, and for all i respectively. To this end, we split ||f_imathbbm1_E_i^c||_L^1 &le ||f_imathbbm1_(R_i^c times R_i+1^c)^c||_L^1 + ||f_imathbbm1_R_i^c times R_i+1^cmathbbm1_E_i^c||_L^1. Denoting f'_i := E(f_i mid P'_i otimes P_i+1'), we now claim that widetildef_i mathbbm1_R_i^c times R_i+1^c le 4 f'_i. Both sides are (P_i otimes P_i+1)-measurable, so we must check the inequality in every part A_i times A_i+1 of P_i otimes P_i+1. If A_i = R_i or A_i+1 = R_i+1, then the left-hand side vanishes. More precisely, our application of crefprop:reduction-to-structure.(iii) produced a partition P of X and a part R in P with P(R) le delta^2, such that E_x_1, ldots, x_k prod_i=1^k E(f mid P otimes P)(x_i,x_i+1) mathbbm1_R^c(x_i) ll_k delta + E_x_1, ldots, x_k mathbbm1_x_1,ldots,x_k textnormal distinctprod_i=1^k f(x_i,x_i+1) le 2delta, and the dense pairs condition was applied for a partition P', obtained by possibly combining R with another part of P. Now fixing some part A in P with A neq R (and thus A cap R = varnothing), and restricting the implied summation in crefeq:reduced-to-structure to those x_1, ldots, x_k in A, we get \[ 2delta gg_k E_x_1, ldots, x_k prod_i=1^k E[f mid A times A] mathbbm1_A(x_i) &= E[f mid A times A]^k E_x_1, ldots, x_k prod_i=1^k mathbbm1_A(x_i) \\ &= E[f mid A times A]^k P(A)^k. \] Summing over A yields \[ sum_substackA in P \\ A neq R E[f mid A times A] P(A)^2 ll_k sum_A in P (2delta)^1/k P(A) = (2delta)^1/k, \] and using the bound ||f||_S^infty le ||f||_S^q_1 le C (coupled with crefeq:Schatten-infty), we further obtain \[ ||f mathbbm1_textnormaldiag(P')||_L^1 &= sum_A in P' E[f mathbbm1_A times A] \\ &le E[f mathbbm1_R times X] + E[f mathbbm1_X times R] + sum_A in P' E[f mathbbm1_(A setminus R) times (A setminus R)] \\ &le 2||f||_S^inftysqrtP(R) + sum_substackA in P \\ A neq R E[f mathbbm1_A times A] \\ &le 2C delta + sum_substackA in P \\ A neq R E[f mid A times A] P(A)^2 ll_k Cdelta + (2delta)^1/k. \] By making delta smaller (if necessary) in terms of epsilon, k, C, we can thus guarantee that ||f mathbbm1_textnormaldiag(P')||_L^1 le epsilon/8. Denote $q := (q_1, \ldots, q_k)$; we will choose a parameter $\delta = \delta(\epsilon, K, k, C) > 0$ later in the proof. \[
    \mathbf{E}_{x_1, \ldots, x_k} \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbf{E}(f_{i} \mid \mathcal{P}_i \otimes \mathcal{P}_{i+1})(x_i, x_{i+1})\mathbbm{1}_{R_i^c}(x_i) 
    \le 
    \delta + \mathbf{E}_{x_1, \ldots, x_k} \prod_{i=1}^k f_{i}(x_i,x_{i+1}).
\]
By \cref{eq:few-k-cycles-1}, the right-hand side is at most $2\delta$.
Now consider, for each $i$, the $(\mathcal{P}_i \otimes \mathcal{P}_{i+1})$-measurable functions
\[ 
\begin{aligned}
    \widetilde{f}_i := \mathbf{E}(f_{i} \mid \mathcal{P}_i \otimes \mathcal{P}_{i+1}) \qquad\quad  \text{and}  \qquad\quad  
    g_i := \frac{\widetilde{f}_i \mathbbm{1}_{\widetilde{f}_i \le 4K}}{4K} \mathbbm{1}_{R_i^c \times R_{i+1}^c}.
\end{aligned}
\] 

It follows that for some constant $c_{K,k} > 0$ depending on $K$ and $k$, we have
\begin{equation}
    \mathbf{E}_{x_1, \ldots, x_k} \prod_{i=1}^k g_i(x_i, x_{i+1}) \le c_{K,k} \delta.
\end{equation}
Note that $0 \le g_i \le 1$ everywhere, so we can apply the dense removal lemma (\cref{thm:dense-k-cycle-removal}) for the probability spaces $(X_i, \Sigma(\mathcal{P}_i), \mathbf{P}_i)$ and the functions $g_i$. We finally pick $\delta = \delta(\epsilon, K, k)$ small enough, as given by \cref{thm:dense-k-cycle-removal}, to find $(\mathcal{P}_{i} \otimes \mathcal{P}_{i+1})$-measurable subsets $E_{i} \subset X_i \times X_{i+1}$ such that
\[
    \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbbm{1}_{E_{i}}(x_i, x_{i+1}) = 0 \qquad\quad \text{and} \qquad\quad  
     ||g_{i} \mathbbm{1}_{E_{i}^c}||_{L^1} \le \frac{\epsilon}{16K},
\]
for all $x_1, \ldots, x_k$, and for all $i$ respectively.

We also make $\delta$ smaller if necessary, in terms of $\epsilon$ and $C$, to guarantee that 
\[
    \delta ||f_i||_{S^\infty} \le \frac{\epsilon}{4}.
\]
(This is possible by the assumed Schatten norm bounds, recalling that $||f_i||_{S^{\infty}} \le ||f_i||_{S^{q_i}} \le C$.)

It remains to show that $||f_{i}\mathbbm{1}_{E_{i}^c}||_{L^1} \le \epsilon$. To this end, we split
\begin{equation} \label{eq:edges-decomposition}
\begin{aligned}
    ||f_{i}\mathbbm{1}_{E_{i}^c}||_{L^1} 
    &\le
    ||f_i\mathbbm{1}_{(R_i^c \times R_{i+1}^c)^c}||_{L^1}
    +
    ||f_i\mathbbm{1}_{R_i^c \times R_{i+1}^c}\mathbbm{1}_{E_{i}^c}||_{L^1}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
We use \cref{eq:Schatten-infty} to bound the first term:
\begin{equation} \label{eq:edges-first-term}
\begin{aligned}
    ||f_i\mathbbm{1}_{(R_i^c \times R_{i+1}^c)^c}||_{L^1}
    &\le 
    ||f_i\mathbbm{1}_{R_i \times X_{i+1}}||_{L^1}
    +
    ||f_i\mathbbm{1}_{X_i \times R_{i+1}}||_{L^1}
    \\
    &\le ||f_i||_{S^\infty} \left(||\mathbbm{1}_{R_i}||_{L^2} + ||\mathbbm{1}_{R_{i+1}}||_{L^2}  \right)
    \\
    &\le 
    ||f_i||_{S^\infty} \left(\sqrt{\mathbf{P}_i(R_i)} + \sqrt{\mathbf{P}_{i+1}(R_{i+1})} \right)
    \le

\end{equation}
To handle the second term in \cref{eq:edges-decomposition}, note that since $\{\widetilde{f}_i \le K\}$, $E_i$ and and $R_i^c \times R_{i+1}^c$ are $(\mathcal{P}_i \otimes \mathcal{P}_{i+1})$-measurable sets, we have

    \\
    &= 
    ||f_i\mathbbm{1}_{\widetilde{f}_i >4K} \mathbbm{1}_{R_i^c \times R_{i+1}^c}||_{L^1}
    +
    ||\widetilde{f}_i\mathbbm{1}_{\widetilde{f}_i \le 4K} \mathbbm{1}_{R_i^c \times R_{i+1}^c} \mathbbm{1}_{E_i^c}||_{L^1}
    \\
    &=
    ||f_i \mathbbm{1}_{\widetilde{f}_i >4K} \mathbbm{1}_{R_i^c \times R_{i+1}^c}||_{L^1}
    +
    ||4K g_i \mathbbm{1}_{E_i^c}||_{L^1}
    \\

\end{aligned}

We are left to handle the term $||\widetilde{f}_i\mathbbm{1}_{\widetilde{f}_i >4K} \mathbbm{1}_{R_i^c \times R_{i+1}^c}||_{L^1}$, and we intend to use the dense pairs condition, recalling that $\widetilde{f}_i = \mathbf{E}(f_i \mid \mathcal{P}_i \otimes \mathcal{P}_{i+1})$.
